articles.title: The Case for Carceral Minimalism
articles.author: Paul Heideman
articles.content: When Karl Marx wrote that the past “weighs like a nightmare on the brains of the living,” he wasn’t talking about 2020, but he may as well have been. That year weighs particularly heavy, it seems, on democratic socialists running for office. Everyone from New York’s Zohran Mamdani to Wisconsin’s Francesca Hong has been confronted with statements they made in that year, generally on the subject of defunding or abolishing police and prisons. In almost every case, democratic socialists have walked back their endorsements of abolition, mindful of the deep unpopularity of the demand. At the same time, a number of socialist writers have developed criticisms of abolition as a strategy. If abolition had a moment in 2020, that moment appears to be over. Yet socialist critics of abolition have not succeeded in articulating a positive framework as an alternative to abolition. This lacuna is made all the more glaring by the insistence of abolitionists that their project flows logically from, and is indeed required by, anti-capitalism. Fortunately, such a framework does exist. It’s called carceral minimalism , and it ultimately provides a better path for realizing socialist ideals than abolition does. The Law of the Weakest Over the last few decades, a number of writers across the world have developed a framework that has been called minimalist criminal law or radical penal minimalism . I prefer “carceral minimalism” as a clearer and more succinct phrase and will use that instead. Legal scholars and social scientists like Máximo Langer, Luigi Ferrajoli, and Loïc Wacquant have argued that while in most societies the coercive footprint of the state should be significantly lessened, eliminating it altogether is not a viable road to social justice. In thinking about the proper structure and scope of police powers for the state, Ferrajoli has argued for a framework he calls the “law of the weakest.” The law, he contends, should prioritize protecting the weakest party in each stage of criminal law. At the moment of offending, the law should prioritize the protection of the victim of crime, whose rights are being trampled by another. However, in both the trial stage and the penal stage, the accused and the convict are now the weakest party, standing more or less helpless before the awesome power of the state. As such, in those contexts, institutions and practices must be structured to protect their rights, since they are the ones most likely to have their rights violated. It’s a very simple framework, and one that is deeply consonant with socialist ideals. Egalitarianism can, as the anthropologist Christopher Boehm has argued , be thought of as its own kind of hierarchy, one in which the weak dominate the strong in order to prevent them from dominating everyone. In egalitarian pre-state societies, this gives rise to a fiercely egalitarian ethos that actively suppresses the acquisition of excessive power by any individual in the group. Equality, in other words, is how the weak guard themselves against domination by the strong. Socialism, in this account, is simply the proactive prevention of domination by those with the most resources. It is the protection of those with the fewest resources, or the economically weakest. Rule by the Strongest If this were all carceral minimalism consisted of, abolitionists might object that it’s not a different framework at all. After all, it’s a core contention of abolitionists that getting rid of police and prisons is the only way to protect the rights of the weakest, the main violator of which, they argue, is the coercive power of the state. Carceral minimalism’s difference with abolition is thus not primarily in the realm of values, but rather in what Vladimir Lenin once called the “concrete analysis of the concrete situation.” Specifically, carceral minimalism asserts two theses concerning how the law of the weakest should be realized that directly conflict with abolitionist arguments. First, carceral minimalism holds that the elimination of the coercive public safety apparatus will worsen the violation of the rights of the weakest, because crime will increase. And the kind of crime that is likely to increase is not simply the kind of victimless crime or crime of circumstances (stealing when one can’t afford food, for example) that abolitionists tend to focus on. Nearly half of the people held in American prisons and jails are there for offenses legally classified as violent. Poverty breeds crime, and it quite often breeds violent crime. There is overwhelming evidence that police, and the threat of imprisonment they carry, do prevent crime. Much of this evidence is presented in social-scientific studies that can be intimidating for lay readers, but the basic line of reasoning is clear enough: people who commit crimes respond to incentives like anyone else, and when the costs of committing a crime rise (because, for example, it is likelier that the perpetrator will get caught), people commit fewer crimes. Police, through both their simple presence in areas where crimes are committed and their role in solving crimes after the fact, raise the likelihood of being caught, which leads to people committing fewer crimes. Abolitionists often respond to this line of argument with their own, which is that it is policing itself that causes the violent crime that it is supposed to prevent. For example, it is often argued that the criminalization of recreational drugs creates a market in which participants must use violence to protect their market and enforce payment. Therefore, abolitionists contend, if drugs were decriminalized, violence would decline and the market for these drugs would be like markets for legal goods. While the logic here is coherent, the implications of this argument are not at all favorable to abolitionists. After all, the reason that most markets are conducted without violence is that participants’ property rights and contracts are enforced by the coercive apparatus of the state. Abolitionists imagine that abolition will lead to the market for drugs becoming like the market for televisions, but the very logic of their argument implies the result will be the opposite — without any state monopoly on coercive power, the market for televisions would become like the market for drugs. In other words, it will be subject to rule by the strongest. Rule by the strongest isn’t simply a problem for potential victims of crime. It’s also a threat to those who commit crimes. A state apparatus can be bureaucratically regulated, such that even if a victim’s family feels the sentence a court imposes is too lenient, there is little they can do about the situation without becoming offenders themselves. But in a situation where the state abdicates its role in coercion, victims and their families are bound by no such institutional framework, and the law of vengeance, itself a form of rule by the strongest, becomes the default. The law of the weakest protects the accused as well, but in order for it to obtain, the state must still retain the apparatus of law. As such, carceral minimalism contends that the coercive apparatus of the state should be radically reduced rather than abolished, in order to protect the rights of the weakest. The Price of Protection The second major difference with abolitionism concerns how the rights of the weakest can be secured in steps two and three of criminal law — that is, trial and confinement. Abolitionists are committed to tearing down the apparatus of both courts and prisons. Many even argue that any increase in the institutional footprint of these structures, such as increasing the number of public defenders or increasing spending on prisons, only legitimizes them and makes them harder to eliminate. Carceral minimalists, by contrast, argue that the law of the weakest will often require devoting more resources to penal institutions. Take prisons. American prisons are plagued by violence, including sexual violence. This violence is an outrageous violation of the rights of the incarcerated. But all the evidence suggests that what is needed to prevent this violence is more resources spent per prisoner — a demand entirely compatible with, and in fact easiest to meet alongside, a far smaller prison population. From the shamefully incomplete data we have on the subject, it appears that Florida prisons are some of the worst in the country for sexual violence against inmates. Florida is also one of the states that spends the very least per prisoner (on an age-adjusted basis). Internationally, we observe a similar pattern. Northern European prisons are significantly less violent than American ones, in part because the ratio of prison staff to prisoners is about one-to-one. In the United States, it’s between one-to-two and one-to-five, depending on the state. In Brazil, where prisons are far more violent than even the United States, it’s about one-to-seven. The conclusion is inescapable: ensuring safety for prisoners requires considerable expenditure. Abolitionists might object that this ignores that prison staff themselves are a frequent source of violence, and one unlikely to be solved by hiring more staff. It’s true that violence against prisoners by staff is rampant in American prisons. From the best data we have, it’s roughly as prevalent as violence by fellow inmates. But looking internationally, we can see that countries that spend considerably more resources per prisoner can do a much better job protecting prisoners’ rights. In Norway, violence against inmates by staff is considerably less common. Part of this is training. Norwegian prison officers receive two years of paid training, and most have attended some college. In California, officers receive thirteen weeks of training. Another component is smaller prisons, which allow more relationship-building between staff and inmates. Both of these cost more money than the American way of incarceration. None of this is to say that more spending per prisoner is sufficient to secure prisoners’ rights. It is perfectly possible to spend more without improving the lot of the incarcerated. And the issue of staff violence against inmates also illustrates the need for effective discipline of staff, a bureaucratic feature not directly tied to funding. But the differences in prisons both in the United States and internationally suggest insistently that it is impossible to secure the rights of the incarcerated without spending much more per prisoner than the United States currently does. Calls to defund the prisons will do little to protect the people inside them. Preserve Only What’s Necessary There is much that abolitionists and carceral minimalists agree on. The American justice system is a concatenation of human rights abuses, from the failure to protect the lives of the poorest people against violence to rampant, unjustifiable violence committed by agents of the state to the warehousing of huge numbers of people in institutions that violate their rights daily. Minimalists would also argue that the policing and punishment apparatus of the state must be shrunk and softened. While, as Christopher Lewis and Adaner Usmani have argued , it is difficult to imagine the United States to achieve Norway-like prison conditions without building a Norway-like welfare state, it is clear that there is room for reform even within the confines of this country’s benighted political economy. For example, during the COVID-19 pandemic, a number of states released large numbers of prisoners to maintain public health in prisons, and the best evidence suggests that this scale of release (generally between 5 and 10 percent of the incarcerated population) did not increase crime. There are two consequences that follow for carceral minimalism. First, whatever the limits of reform under capitalism may be, we have not yet reached them. Further work to reduce the prison population by reducing sentence length or using alternatives to incarceration (from fines to community service) must be pursued. Second, in order for the American criminal justice system to live up to the demands of the law of the weakest, a broader challenge to the power of American capitalism is necessary. It’s a vision of criminal justice that is both achievable in the short term and congruent with socialists’ deepest values.

articles.title: Centrist Dems Really Do Hate the Left More Than Trump
articles.author: Branko Marcetic
articles.content: For a good while into the second Donald Trump presidency, centrist Democrats were nowhere to be found. Their strategy was, in the immortal words of former Bill Clinton campaign strategist James Carville, to “roll over and play dead” and simply wait and hope that the Trump administration would collapse in popularity without them having to do anything.A year and a half later, Trump’s approval rating is in the toilet, some of the most divisive primary contests are over, and there are only three months to go until the midterm elections that may well decide not just the future of Trump’s presidency but the entire country’s political trajectory. So the average Democratic voter will be heartened to learn that — as the smoke clears after the bitter Michigan primary contest and its two rival Democratic candidates make up and vow to join forces for the general election — centrist Democrats have suddenly come back to life, gearing up to wage relentless war against their political opponents to the tune of $15 million.No, not Republicans. The political opponents that have the centrist Democrats newly energized and willing to fight like hell are the democratic socialists who have become a powerful organizing force within their party and some of its most popular national figures. That’s according to the New York Times, which reported yesterday that the centrist organization Third Way, in concert with unnamed “moderates,” plan to launch a “discrediting campaign” lasting from now until 2028 that takes aim at the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), the group whose members include Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani and is a key part of the coalition behind the party’s Senate candidate in Michigan, Abdul El-Sayed. That campaign will see Third Way not just do opposition research into DSA and target its elected officials but also go after politicians like El-Sayed, who don’t identify as socialists but make common cause with the group.“We are preparing for the next war that is coming,” Third Way’s president, Jonathan Cowan, told the Times about the campaign. This is a month after Cowan and Third Way’s executive vice president, Matt Bennett, warned in the Washington Post that DSA was “not a faction to be appeased,” urging the party to “fight” the group by pledging “money, organization, and spine.”It’s a well-worn joke at this point that Democratic centrists fight the Left harder than they fight the far right. But here, Third Way and whatever “moderates” are part of this effort are actually giving us an honest-to-God, real-life example of it: centrist Democrats’ big play to push back against Trump’s wrecking ball of a presidency was to literally do nothing. Third Way itself has been largely invisible, other than to make a list of words Democrats shouldn’t use, lead a public campaign against leftist streamer Hasan Piker, and tell Dems to be more hawkish. But now that the Left is winning elections, they are jumping into action, pledging to “fight” a “war” and calling on Democrats to show “spine.” You can’t make this stuff up.Of course, the Third Wayers frame this around the concern that socialists and the progressives allied with them will cost the party future elections to Trump. Well, too late for that: Bennett himself gushed in 2024 about how Kamala Harris was positioning herself as a centrist, her efforts to win disaffected Republicans, and that “she has not made a single mistake,” all before that campaign handed the White House keys to Trump — and did it by winning fewer Republican voters than Joe Biden had.You almost start to suspect that maybe there’s something else going on here. Like, maybe, the fact that DSA and its progressive allies’ hostility to big money in politics and support for taxing the rich and corporations might constitute a threat to an organization like Third Way.After all, as Bennett himself cheerfully admitted more than a decade ago, “the majority” of Third Way’s funding comes from its board of trustees, most of them former Wall Street executives, who “write us personal checks.” Not much has changed: its trustees today overwhelmingly serve in or come out of the corporate world, venture capital, or the world of finance, including private equity firms like Warburg Pincus and investment banks like Morgan Stanely.A Sludge investigation last year determined that the organization’s donors are still made up of “a web of billionaire liberal megadonors, Democratic dark money funnelers, Fortune 500 CEOs, and corporations with plenty to gain from a more corporate-friendly Democratic Party.”Meanwhile, the organization has, from the moment Trump took office, explicitly urged Democrats to “move away from the dominance of small-dollar donors” — in other words, rely more on the corporate and billionaire money that funds its own work and whose role in US politics disgusts Americans across the political spectrum. You can see why: according to its most recent 990 filing, thanks to this money, the median salary of Third Way executives like Cowan and Bennett is $296,343.Whatever it is exactly that drives Third Way and its associated party “moderates,” there is no way that their anti-DSA campaign — timed at the precise moment that most rank-and-file Democrats and even its party officials are focused on unity and beating Republicans in the midterms — is not going to hurt their own party and help the GOP. After all, Third Way is explicitly planning to attack the Democrats’ own candidate in a key swing state, while its attacks on DSA more broadly will not just serve as a distraction from key policy debates that hands ammunition to the Right but will also discourage any alliance between nonsocialist candidates and DSA, whose electoral ground game is recognized even by its detractors as uniquely effective.But this is the crux of it: centrist Democrats are clearly willing to tear apart their own party and hand power to the forces behind Trump, as long as it means stopping the Left from having any power. It’s all especially rich after weeks of establishment pundits accusing socialists of a sinister “factional” agenda that makes defeating centrists a higher priority than beating the Right.That doesn’t mean this effort is going to work, of course. In fact, it could backfire on them spectacularly. Centrists are in this situation in the first place because their “roll over and play dead” strategy disgusted their own voter base. And they’re now picking this intraparty fight at the exact time that socialists and their ideas have strong purchase within the Democratic Party.Roughly a third of Democrats and independents who lean toward the party identify as democratic socialists, and 73 percent of Democratic-leaning voters would be fine with the party nominating a self-described democratic socialist (including 20 percent who would be “enthusiastic” about it). Another recent poll found 52 percent of Democrats believe socialists have some good ideas, not much different to the proportion of Republicans who say the same about MAGA politicians. Socialist politicians Bernie Sanders and Zohran Mamdani are, after Barack Obama, the two most popular politicians in the country, beating out the Democratic Party itself.Third Way’s plan is presumably to try and change this. But a bunch of money and white papers from a Wall Street–funded outfit defaming the party’s own standard-bearers at the precise time its voters are fixated on defeating Republicans may not have that effect. It may just end up making the political dividing lines clearer — and reveal the true priorities of the party’s corporate wing.

articles.title: Make No Mistake—The Left Is on a Winning Streak
articles.content: Something has shifted among the Democratic electorate. That was already clear from Zohran Mamdani’s trouncing of establishment royalty Andrew Cuomo in the New York mayoral race last year, punctuated by a series of yet more socialist wins over establishment incumbents seven months later. And it was clear from the primary election in Maine, where Democratic voters rejected their own governor in favor of a left-populist firebrand dogged by scandals who had never held political office. But the victory of Abdul El-Sayed in Michigan over the Israel lobby – backed centrist Rep. Haley Stevens may eclipse even these as both a victory for the broad Left and for anyone who genuinely cares about democracy. No candidate has been outspent to the degree El-Sayed was and still won, however narrowly, with Stevens’s nine-to-one advantage in outside spending funding an endless torrent of TV ads touting a nonexistent endorsement from former President Barack Obama and scurrilously attacking El-Sayed. Former socialist lawmaker Jamaal Bowman fell in 2024 to a money landslide roughly a quarter of the scale of what El-Sayed faced. Besides a visceral reminder that it is possible for people power to triumph over naked plutocracy, the results should also help, depending on what happens in November, put to bed the very last talking point that party centrists held over their progressive opponents: that socialists and other lefty candidates only have appeal on the coasts or in deep-blue urban areas. This was never true, as we knew from countless indicators: Sen. Bernie Sanders’s 2016 primary win in Michigan, for instance, or the fact that two of the earliest ​ “ Squad” wins came in Detroit with Rashida Tlaib and Minneapolis with Ilhan Omar, along with the spate of local- and state-level socialist victories in the Midwest over the past decade, including the socialist blocs in the Chicago and Minneapolis city councils. But given the Senate race’s statewide nature and in a state that Trump has won twice, El-Sayed is now in a position to put that talking point to rest in the eyes of the average voter in a way that none of these other electoral milestones could have. Still, denial is a hard thing to shake. ​ “ Progressives didn’t get the big election night they wanted,” read an early Wednesday headline from Politico. Wednesday morning saw a hurried, collective moving of goalposts by Left-averse commentators to absurdly redefine victory as not actually winning the election, as El-Sayed did, but winning it by a blowout margin. In reality, it’s hard to make the argument that Michigan handed the Left a bad night. Five out of six of Bernie Sanders’ endorsed candidates won in the state, including Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) member Donavan McKinney, who will almost certainly become what will potentially be the ninth socialist member of the U.S. House from the safe blue seat in Michigan’s 13 th Congressional District, and expand the left-wing ​ “ Squad” to as many as dozens of members. Also notable is Sunrise Movement cofounder William Lawrence, who won his three-way race for the purple Seventh Congressional District — previously held by centrist Democratic senator Elissa Slotkin, whose endorsed candidate for the seat came in third last night. Also victorious among Sanders endorsees was Abbas Alawieh , a cofounder of the Uncommitted Movement and an uncommitted delegate at last year’s Democratic National Convention who led a sit-in in Chicago in protest of the Kamala Harris campaign’s position on the Gaza genocide, and who won his primary for state senate with a comfortable 18 -point margin. That list also includes two other DSA members: County Commissioner Yousef Rabhi, who handily defeated the sitting, four-term mayor of Ann Arbor, and Chris Gilmer-Hill, who was endorsed by both El-Sayed and the organization’s Metro Detroit branch and won his primary to represent Michigan’s 8 th District in the state house. If this isn’t the night that progressives had wanted, then we can only assume they had wanted to lose. Two birds with one stone But it’s El-Sayed’s victory that is deservedly being treated as the most important story of the night. The result marks another high-profile rejection of the Democratic elite by their previously loyal voters, arguably the story of the party during the Trump 2 . 0 era. Establishment Democrats went all in to try and swing the race to Stevens, with Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer securing donor support for her and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Sen. Kristen Gillibrand — who last year falsely accused Mamdani of talking about ​ “ global jihad” — reportedly lying to donors that the other centrist in the race was a DSA member. A spate of 11 th -hour endorsements from big Democratic names, including the still- popular Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer and the mystifyingly prominent Rep. Jim Clyburn , couldn’t push Stevens over the line. Her centrist colleague, Rep. Hillary Scholten, trashed El-Sayed as a misogynist and ​ “ anti-American ” and even suggested she might not back him in the general. (Scholten, who this year ran unopposed, is now in a potentially vulnerable place, with El-Sayed having won 58 % of the vote in three Western Michigan counties with parts contained in her district). But arguably, the most significant thing about the race is the sheer scale of right-wing money El-Sayed had to overcome to win — and the massive defeat of the pro-Israel lobby that it represents. Only a few years ago, pro-Israel forces were virtually dictating the results of Democratic primaries through unheard-of levels of outside spending against otherwise well-liked progressives. Stevens herself was one of the beneficiaries of this strategy. In 2022 , she cruised to victory over the progressive son of one of Michigan’s most famous political families, former Rep. Andy Levin, on the back of a more than $ 3 million investment from the United Democracy Project (UDP), the super PAC of the American Israel Political Affairs Committee (AIPAC). While UDP funded an anti-Levin ad blitz that never actually mentioned Israel, the then-president of AIPAC openly attacked Levin — a proud Zionist and former synagogue president, whose transgression was pushing to condition U.S. aid to Israel as a way to stop it from destroying the two-state solution — as the ​ “ most corrosive member of Congress to the US-Israel relationship.” Stevens ended up winning the district, which contains much of her home county of Oakland, by nearly 20 points. Considered an ominous sign for money in politics at the time, that amount was a small fraction of the nearly $ 32 million that the pro-Israel UDP invested in Stevens this time around, the largest sum it has ever spent on any congressional race. Together with another $ 30 million from groups funded by various corporate interests, it made the race the state’s most expensive nonpresidential primary on record and the third-most expensive Senate primary ever held. And this time, the issue of Israel was front and center — not so much in the ads that UDP ran but in the fundamental political divide between the two candidates and the metacommentary surrounding it. Just like Cuomo had in New York, Stevens bet big on bear-hugging Israel at a time when the country has never had a worse standing with the U.S. public, and tried to make an issue of El-Sayed’s criticism of its treatment of Gazans and his association with other Israel critics like Hasan Piker — even at one point all but calling him an antisemite. And just like Cuomo in New York, the strategy entirely misread where the Democratic electorate is after 2024 . This time, ​ “ Oakland County’s congresswoman ” only won Oakland County — where she was born, raised, and currently lives and that she represents in Congress — by 6 points, well below her winning margin in 2022 . Together with the victories of Alawieh and McKinney — who prevailed against an incumbent who became a born-again Israel Firster, dragging his feet on backing a ceasefire and disavowing DSA after October 7 — the race is the most dramatic confirmation we’ve seen so far that the politics around the U.S.-Israel relationship have fundamentally changed, particularly on the Democratic side. Even with a transformed Democratic electorate, it’s unlikely El-Sayed and the forces behind him could have achieved this result without some strategic pragmatism. El-Sayed got the crucial backing of many DSA members on the ground even though he made explicitly clear he was not a socialist. Michigan’s democratic socialists seem to have calculated that the areas where they overlapped, including El-Sayed’s full-throated support for Medicare for All, taxing the rich, and public ownership of artificial-intelligence firms, made his campaign a cause worth supporting — a big-tent approach made easier by the fact that El-Sayed publicly embraced DSA’s support as part of his own broad coalition. El-Sayed, meanwhile, wisely changed his tune in some places even as he held fast to the core policy positions that put him in the crosshairs of big-money, right-wing spenders. He walked back his years-old support for the ​ “ Defund the Police” slogan, winning the endorsement of the Wayne County Deputy Sheriff’s Association, much as Bernie Sanders had once done to engineer his own career-making political upset. And he campaigned with a positive , patriotic style, framing his criticism of Israel around a left-wing version of an ​ “ America First” pitch, undermining the inevitable attempts to paint him as a violent or dangerous ​ “ foreign” extremist. On that note, the history-making nature of El-Sayed’s candidacy, as a proud Muslim and Arab American who leaned into those parts of his background, merits a brief mention. It would be no small thing to have the first-ever Muslim U.S. senator at a time of virulent and rising Islamophobia and anti-Arab racism. That bigotry is lately finding physical form not just in people’s daily remarks, attitudes, and random outbursts of violence but also in actual policy and political rhetoric: Trump’s Muslim ban, his various wars on the Muslim world, the increasingly openly racist rhetoric of establishment policymakers. And it’s not just on the Right. El-Sayed weathered one of the nastier dog-whistling campaigns we’ve seen in a while, a Democratic version of the subtly racist campaign John McCain ran against the not-actually-Muslim Obama eighteen years ago, a campaign that similarly saw El-Sayed’s opponent occasionally come face-to-face with the ugliness it had stirred up. This kind of thing is likely not going away anytime soon, even with this result. But El-Sayed’s victory, as well as his chance to overcome the more openly racist version of this that Republicans seem dead-set on running for the general election, will be an important milestone for basic decency and a more tolerant United States. As things move to the general election, we can say two things for sure: we will keep hearing that the Left is headed for almost certain doom; and AIPAC and other vehicles for big money will spend ever more insane amounts to try and make it a reality. But El-Sayed’s primary win is a reminder that, sometimes, with enough hard work, it’s possible to break through a tsunami of cash and come out breathing on the other side. This story was first posted at Jacobin .

articles.title: The Left Can’t Win Without an Internationalist Vision
articles.author: Salar Mohandesi
articles.content: As we enter a new age of imperial wars, internationalism is very much back on the Left’s agenda. But what is internationalism? And why does it matter? The Left’s preoccupation with “internationalism” stems from the fact that its political project has always been tied in some way to what might be called universal emancipation. To emancipate is to free someone or something from a power, and universal emancipation stands for the liberation of everyone from all domination. The aim of the Left, in other words, is not simply to redistribute wealth, expand state services, or roll back racial discrimination in one’s own country; it is to abolish every form of oppression and domination everywhere. By definition, universal emancipation has to be global or not at all. A World of States But the globe is not a single, smooth, uniform space. The people of the world are not subject to a single administrative entity, set of laws, or police force. Nor are they under the authority of an undifferentiated class of rulers. The planet is instead divided into many distinct political units that have largely taken the form of nation-states. It is precisely these independent nation-states that have assumed primary responsibility for maintaining domination in the world today. This doesn’t mean that the state is the only source of domination, but rather that states are the main enforcers in this inegalitarian world. Whether one fights racism, patriarchy, or capitalism, one will ultimately have to confront the laws, police, courts, and prisons of the state. Since state power is distributed across so many different nation-states, the fight for emancipation takes the form of a multiplicity of different struggles within and against each of the many different nation-states across the globe. This is one of the reasons why the Left has historically tended to speak of “internationalism” rather than, for example, “cosmopolitanism.” The term is a reminder that the ambition to remake the world has to take into account the unavoidable reality that the main political units of the existing world order are nation-states. Even in today’s supposedly globalized world, replete as it is with NGOs, military pacts, transnational corporations, and international institutions, the path to the planetary has to pass through a confrontation with the nation-state. Internationalism is not a moral injunction to help those in need, and neither is it a single ready-made strategy for freeing the world. It instead names the wide range of political problems that emerge from the tension between needing to make change on a global scale and having to strategically take the many nation-states of the world as the primary battlefields. Border Crossings No nation-state has ever governed a single coherent populace. This is largely because states were historically imposed on already heterogeneous populations. These people did not cross into the new nation-states; the recently invented borders of these nation-states “crossed” them. These nation-states can never be hermetically sealed: millions of people regularly traverse their borders, and many countries are home to immigrants from other states. This adds to the fundamental heterogeneity at the heart of every nation-state. Quite a few countries are now largely composed of people whose ancestors were born in other parts of the world. Since every state is home to a diverse population, meaningful emancipatory change depends on finding ways to bring different people together in common struggle — people who were born in different nation-states, who speak different languages, reside in different places, live in different communities, and care about different issues. Yet the ruling bloc in every country always strives to prevent that unity from being forged. Division is how rulers maintain their domination, and the most effective way to accomplish disunity is to mobilize invented political categories such as race, nationality, or especially citizenship to transform these real differences into insurmountable divisions. Today the ruling blocs that govern the countries of the world are attempting to neutralize popular discontent by channeling political anger into xenophobic nativism. This strategy can even turn immigrants against one another, including those from the same country. The United States is probably the best example of this, but it is by no means unique. In this way, one can say that internationalism begins within the nation-state itself. Each nation-state governs a heterogeneous population and legally recodes these differences as ones of nationality. Since these “national” divisions are used to turn people against one another within a fundamentally “multinational” state, effective political work within a nation-state is always already international. Global Solutions In addition to impeding unification within a given nation-state, the partition of the globe into national borders, national identities, and nation-states make it much harder to organize a unified movement across borders. Although these sharp divisions do not turn everyone into a xenophobe, they tend to narrow the political horizon in a way that encourages people in any given country to prioritize domestic issues over international ones. This is especially true in the heartlands of insulated imperialist countries such as the United States, where the political system is designed to cultivate a culture of ruthless individualism. If people in these countries do become politicized, it is often — though of course not always — because developments within their own nation-state have had a direct impact on their lives. Gas prices are increasing, groceries are becoming too expensive, employers are monitoring their social media accounts, unprecedented floods are damaging their home, or immigration police are disrupting their neighborhoods. These are all legitimate reasons to turn to leftist politics, and they are deeply entangled with global processes. But the internationalist dimensions of these grievances are deliberately obscured. The challenge is to connect the dots. Those who care about emancipation have to explain that local issues are rooted in a global context, and therefore can only be solved globally. They have to convince people that what happens abroad does affect them, and so their fate is bound up with millions of people they will never meet. A Plurality of Struggles Once people choose to concern themselves with struggles elsewhere, there is a great deal they can do to help. In almost every case, those who fight oppression and domination will find themselves sorely outgunned by the ruling bloc in their state. This bloc controls vast arsenals, trained police forces, overflowing war chests, and extensive media apparatuses. Solidarity can shift the balance of power. It can help comrades fighting in other countries feel that they are not alone. It can spread the word about their struggles, focus the international spotlight on the injustices that they face, and prevent other states from intervening. It can supply them with funds, information, equipment, training, bases, advisers, even volunteers. The best way to help struggles abroad, however, is not just to provide aid, but also to wage struggles at home. When antiwar activists in the 1960s asked what they could do to help the people of Vietnam, Vietnamese revolutionaries used to say: make revolution in your own country. Che Guevara famously translated this idea as creating “ two, three, many Vietnams .” Solidarity is not simply about lending a hand to people struggling elsewhere but multiplying struggles at home. If the only way to change the world is to wage struggles in the many different nation-states that make up the globe, then the question is how to coordinate this plurality of struggles. Different countries have different laws, histories, popular cultures, intellectual traditions, state systems, organizations, institutions, economies, and political forces. Each country, in other words, has its own distinct terrain of struggle, which in turn informs how struggles there will develop. This is not to say that struggles in different countries are completely closed off from one another. Those involved in such struggles are almost always aware of one another, and sometimes in touch. But the unification of these heterogenous struggles on so many distinct national terrains into a common international movement is never a given. How can the Left coordinate them? Internationalism From Above Leftists are not the only ones who have organized across borders. The ruling blocs of the various states have also historically coordinated their efforts, especially when faced with revolutionary threats. The challenge of communism after World War II, for instance, compelled the many different ruling blocs of the world to put aside their differences and assist one another. To contain the common threat, they established a number of interstate economic, financial, diplomatic, and military alliances coordinated by the United States. Many of these rulers willingly accepted US leadership as the primary guardian of the inegalitarian capitalist world order. The United States not only created the conditions for the endless expansion of capitalism, but also propped up vulnerable states fending off liberation struggles, directly intervened against emancipatory movements, and overthrew revolutionaries after they seized power. The United States is no longer as powerful as it once was, but it is still the dominant military force in the world, and it still has the ability, and will, to intervene anywhere in the world to crush emancipatory struggles. So long as this US-led imperialist alliance exists, emancipatory struggles everywhere will be imperiled. Even if leftists succeed in bringing down a repressive state, they will still be menaced by coups, sanctions, sabotage, air strikes, and diplomatic isolation. The need to survive these threats will likely force them to adopt draconian measures, which will in turn undermine their emancipatory aims. This might lead them to restrict civil liberties to prevent subversion, reallocate limited resources into defense, and treat dissent as conspiracies organized from abroad. What, then, must leftists across the world do to successfully hold off the inevitable onslaught of this US-led imperial alliance? Interstate Rivalries Although virtually every ruling bloc today is committed to preventing a future without domination, and although these blocs often coordinate to keep emancipatory movements everywhere at bay, this does not mean they are on the best of terms. One of the functions of the postwar US-led imperial alliance was to impose discipline on these constantly competing ruling blocs so that they could better resist the common menace of emancipatory movements. Today that alliance is fracturing , and wars between rival ruling blocs are becoming more frequent. Moreover, there are some nation-states today that are capitalist, patriarchal, inegalitarian, and in some cases authoritarian but which nevertheless oppose the United States and its imperial alliance. This presents a dilemma for those committed to universal emancipation. On the one hand, the goal of ending all domination requires the overthrow of these inegalitarian states, even if they happen to reject US imperial hegemony. On the other hand, the United States remains the single greatest threat to emancipatory movements everywhere. Although leftists are presently too weak to decisively intervene in these interstate rivalries, their internationalist commitments raise the question of how they should relate to such thorny political situations. Does supporting popular uprisings against states at odds with the United States inadvertently create pretexts for Washington to invade their countries? Does the need to resist the shared enemy of US imperialism end up giving succor to these inegalitarian anti-US regimes? Is there another way out ? The Problem of Internationalism The nation-state is incompatible with emancipation. The state’s primary function is to maintain the inegalitarian status quo, which it does by sustaining the ruling bloc, absorbing internal challenges, repressing liberation struggles, dividing the populace, and extinguishing the space for political experimentation. Anyone who fights for emancipation must therefore find a way out of the nation-state. Internationalism therefore points to a final fundamental strategic problem inherent to emancipatory politics today. As Richard Seymour summarizes: universal emancipation means overcoming the state, but the division of the world into sovereign nation-states means strategically taking those states as the principal site of struggle.

articles.title: DSA Has Arrived
articles.author: Detroit DSA
articles.content: By Madeline W. Detroit will become the first U.S. city to be fully represented by democratic socialists in Congress, following the wins of Rashida Tlaib and Donavan McKinney Metro Detroit DSA endorsed four candidates in local races and eked out wins in all four, flexing the political muscle the likes of which NYC-DSA and Denver DSA demonstrated a month ago in their barrage of wins across endorsed races. Cadre candidate and environmental advocate Chris Gilmer-Hill ran against incumbent Democrat Helena Scott in Michigan’s 8th State House District — covering areas of Ferndale, Pleasant Ridge, and Northwest Detroit — and won by 6 percentage points. In an election season increasingly defined by the role of corporate money in politics, Scott was a vulnerable candidate due to her close relationship with DTE and corporate interests. Gilmer-Hill ran on a progressive platform, stumping for key DSA priorities like taking on DTE, enacting Medicare for All, and expanding socialized housing access and protection. Gilmer-Hill will face Republican Bruce Langran in the November general election. By far the most ambitious campaign for Metro Detroit DSA this primary was Donavan McKinney’s campaign to unseat incumbent Democrat Shri Thanedar in Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, encompassing all of Grosse Pointe, all of Detroit, and some of the Down River cities. Thanedar, a Metro Detroit DSA member until his expulsion a few years ago, had become embattled in recent years due to unpopular political positions in a district that was historically held by the late Democratic Socialist John Conyers. Last year, Thanedar voted with House Republicans to “thank” ICE for their mass deportation regime. McKinney sought endorsement from DSA in late spring and was formally approved by the chapter body in June, giving MD-DSA just a few months to build campaign infrastructure capable of beating Thanedar — a monumental undertaking with so little time. The path to victory the chapter saw was not straightforward, but his race had one main factor going for it: significant parts of his district overlapped geographically with Chris Gilmer-Hill’s State House race, making it easy to quickly ramp up McKinney’s campaign work in the area. Combined, DSA knocked 50K doors for Chris Gilmer-Hill and Donavan McKinney. That, along with critical support from fellow socialists in office, Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib and State Representative Dylan Wegela, propelled McKinney to victory. Early this morning, McKinney was declared the winner of his primary contest, winning by 4 percentage points. In the November general election, McKinney will face Republican challenger TP Nykoriak to become the next Congressman in what is a deep blue district. Elsewhere in Metro Detroit, incumbent Democratic Socialists, Congresswoman Rashida Tlaib and State Representative Dylan Wegela, cruised to victory. They will face James Hooper and Chris Dobis, respectively, in the November general election. Michigan is seen as a prime battleground in a proxy war playing out in the Democratic Party nationally between progressives and Democratic Socialists, and the establishment Democratic base. Today, we can now confidently say that Michigan has spoken: DSA is here to stay. Madeline is the co-editor for The Detroit Socialist and a member of Groundwork. DSA Has Arrived was originally published in The Detroit Socialist on Medium, where people are continuing the conversation by highlighting and responding to this story.

articles.title: Uncovering America’s Forgotten Massacre in the Philippines
articles.author: Kim Wagner
articles.content: In March 1906, US troops climbed the volcanic crater of Bud Dajo on the island of Jolo in the southern Philippines and killed a thousand Moro men, women, and children who had resisted American colonial authority. The event was celebrated by US officials as a military victory, and photographs of the dead circulated as souvenirs, postcards, and trophies. Today Bud Dajo is almost entirely absent from American historical memory. In his new book , Massacre in the Clouds , Kim Wagner reconstructs the massacre and the machinery of denial that followed it. Wagner shows how US empire turned mass killing into a heroic “battle” and how that lie survived for more than a century. Historian Michael G. Vann spoke with Wagner about Bud Dajo, American colonial violence, atrocity photography, anti-Muslim racism, and why forgetting is never innocent. Michael G. Vann For readers unfamiliar with Bud Dajo, can you briefly walk us through what happened in March 1906? Who were the Moros in the crater, why were they there, and what did US forces believe they were confronting? Kim Wagner The Bud Dajo operation was one of a series of punitive expeditions that took place after the end of the Philippine-American War, as the United States tried to assert its authority in the southern Philippines. This went on for more than a decade. Every time American forces marched through the islands and burned villages, they claimed this would be the final campaign against the Moros. Then, the following year, they would do it all over again. The Moros who retreated to Bud Dajo in 1906 refused to submit to American authority. They refused to pay the secular head tax, and they opposed the fact that the sultan of Sulu, their own leader, had become an ally of the Americans. In a very literal sense, they tried to remove themselves from American rule by retreating to a remote mountaintop. But American authorities saw that as a direct challenge. That is why you then get a narrative of “outlaws” threatening the law-abiding population and the claim that one final battle was necessary to finish them off. Michael G. Vann The event is often called the “Battle of Bud Dajo,” but your book frames it as a massacre. What is at stake in that language? Kim Wagner It was reported as a battle in the United States at the time — and that’s how it is described on Wikipedia today. You see the same thing with Wounded Knee. Calling it a battle is a conventional way of turning an atrocity into something that allows for a heroic narrative. Three Medals of Honor were awarded after Bud Dajo, and the operation is celebrated with a campaign streamer on the US Army flag. So language was central to the cover-up — it transformed mass violence into military valor. That is why the choice of words matters so much. We see similar disputes today when people argue over whether something should be called a genocide. The terminology shapes the public meaning of the event, and the prevalent use of euphemisms and the passive tense is responsible for far more violence than we usually acknowledge. Michael G. Vann Your book reconstructs the massacre in close detail. What surprised you most as you worked through the military reports, photographs, letters, and colonial records? Kim Wagner The well-known photograph from Bud Dajo was only one image among many, and I found something like thirty or forty other images. There were actually three photographers present, and the iconic image of the trench is not even the most graphic one. There are worse photographs, if you can believe it. At first, I was not sure I would be able to tell the story, because the American authorities did such a thorough job of burying it. They controlled the trans-Pacific cable and could effectively suppress the story while the official military reports were carefully doctored to downplay civilian casualties. But the US soldiers wrote letters home, and those letters were not censored. By trawling through contemporary American newspapers, I found accounts in which soldiers would write home with ordinary details and an opening like “Dear Mom, I’m in the Philippines, I’m enjoying myself,” but then proceed to describe extreme violence, using racial slurs and language that framed the Moros as savage enemies to be exterminated. That was when I realized there was a story to tell beyond the official record. There is also an oral tradition in Jolo today among descendants of the Moros. I managed to visit Bud Dajo and talk to some of the descendants, and that was really important as I did not want American soldiers to have the final word. Michael G. Vann What did the local perspective add? Kim Wagner The local traditions are in the form of songs, almost like epic poems. They do not always clearly distinguish between the Spanish and American periods and are stories about heroic sacrifice by Moros, within an Islamic framework, who refused to submit to Christian invaders. So the narrative is stylized and formalized. But what you get from those traditions is a sense that this was not simply a refusal to submit to American authority. These were people taking a stand for a way of life they saw as threatened. For all their rhetoric of nonintervention, the Americans had completely transformed Moro society and upended many of the traditions that formed its backbone. To the Americans, however, such resistance to colonial rule could never be accepted as legitimate. Michael G. Vann One of the most disturbing aspects of Bud Dajo is that it was photographed. How did the images function at the time — as evidence, trophy, warning, scandal? Kim Wagner The key photograph was taken by a local American photographer who made a living by producing tourist images of Moro life — Orientalist photographs for visitors. He happened to be present during the expedition. There were also two other photographers there with cameras. At this point in time, the line between amateur photography, tourist photography, and official photography was very fluid. The photographer, who had the improbable trade name of Aeronaut Gibbs, captured this scene on the final day of the massacre, after almost every Moro had been killed. We see the soldiers are posing and facing the camera. This is not a snapshot in the modern sense of war photography. It is part of the violence, and that is what makes it a trophy image: soldiers posing with the dead bodies of people they had killed. Not too different from how hunters pose with their prey — or how some soldiers today take selfies in the middle of a battlezone. The photograph from Bud Dajo later became one of Gibbs’s most popular postcards. He reproduced and sold it, and it circulated widely. I found copies in the private papers and photo albums of American officers, including some of the highest-ranking officials in the Philippines. Leonard Wood, the commanding officer, had some of the most graphic images in his family album. On one page, you see his children with a nanny from the Philippines or riding horses on the beach; then you turn the page and see Bud Dajo. That tells us something about the normality of this kind of violence. These images were not understood by many Americans as evidence of atrocity. Michael G. Vann You and I have both worked with images of racialized colonial violence. In fact, that’s how we met many years ago. We recently spent several days with the staff of the My Lai Massacre museum and memorial in Vietnam, discussing their displays of photographs both in the secular Communist Party–run museum and in the Buddhist prayer hall. I’ve always been impressed with how thoughtful you are when engaging such documents as historical artifacts. What responsibilities do historians have when writing about atrocity photographs? Kim Wagner In a general sense, I don’t think we know what to do with such images, and we are still not very good at “reading” them. It is important to consider the ethical implications of reproducing images of racialized violence, for sure. But I also think that refusing to look can become a kind of evasion. The American authorities later tried to destroy the most incriminating image. So we have to ask whose interests are served if we hide it now, even if our intentions today are admirable. Susan Sontag made an important point about Abu Ghraib: the posing of tortured prisoners recalled lynching photographs. That historical perspective is precisely why we need to look closely at these images and dwell on them. Some people have accused me of indulging in war pornography. I think that comes from a superficial way of thinking about atrocity photographs. If all you see are dead bodies and a source of trauma, you cut yourself off from a crucial historical source. This image shows the soldiers who carried out the massacre, posing, and they then sent it home to their families. It is incriminating not just of the act itself but of their mindset. If we want to understand why atrocities happen — how supposedly liberal nations can kill civilians and think nothing of it — we cannot afford to look away. Michael G. Vann How did US officials justify the killing of women and children at Bud Dajo? Kim Wagner It is interesting because they actually did have to justify the killing of women (nobody seemed to care much for the children). They could not simply get away with it. After all, this was only sixteen years after Wounded Knee. In American political culture, the definition of “savage” warfare had long included indiscriminate violence against women and children, yet the very notion of innocence was highly gendered. At first, the US Army denied that women had been killed. Then officials said women were collateral damage, hit by artillery from a distance. Finally, they admitted women had been killed but claimed the soldiers could not tell they were women because they were wearing trousers. The cover-up ended by asserting that these women had been fired up by religious fanaticism. By not conforming to expected feminine behavior, they supposedly lost their protected status as women and became legitimate targets. The Army could then say: yes, women were killed, but we had no choice because they acted like men and were just as dangerous. That argument tied directly into ideas of Muslims as irrational, fanatical, and uniquely dangerous enemies. Michael G. Vann The subtitle of your book is An American Atrocity and the Erasure of History . How does an atrocity that was photographed and reported become forgotten? Kim Wagner We can look around the world today and see how easily people can watch mass violence unfolding before their eyes and deny that it is happening. Atrocities are not difficult to deny — in the past or in the present. There was a cover-up that went all the way to President Theodore Roosevelt, and parts of the press helped bury the story. The San Francisco earthquake also cleared the headlines, which mattered because San Francisco was the forward base of American empire in the Pacific. But it was a strange cover-up because it happened in plain sight. There were newspaper headlines; there were debates in Senate. Both Mark Twain and W. E. B. Du Bois commented on the affair — though not publicly. Ultimately, the fate of a thousand men, women and children on a faraway island was not enough to capture the attention of the American public. And that’s still pretty much the way it is today. The forgetting is not passive. It is a matter of choice. Raoul Peck says in his film Exterminate All the Brutes that knowledge is not what we lack. The problem is the willingness to confront uncomfortable facts. Michael G. Vann Many Americans know about Wounded Knee and My Lai , which you are currently writing about, but not Bud Dajo. What does that absence tell us about how Americans remember empire? Kim Wagner Bud Dajo was arguably the worst massacre of its kind. More people were killed there than at Wounded Knee and My Lai combined, and yet, as you say, it is almost completely forgotten. One thing to note is that even Wounded Knee and My Lai are remembered in a very particular way. They are recognized only as isolated episodes and framed as exceptions that prove the rule of America as a benign or progressive force. The emphasis becomes rogue officers, poorly trained soldiers, or “bad apples.” In one documentary, for instance, Ken Burns describes the Sand Creek Massacre of 1864 as a “dark chapter” or a “shameful moment,” and that is what I would call historical containment. You acknowledge atrocities that cannot be explained away, but only as discrete episodes. There is never an acknowledgment that they are part of a broader pattern, and a larger history, of indiscriminate or exterminatory violence. Bud Dajo was buried because powerful interests wanted it buried. But the amnesia has lasted because for too many Americans, it is preferable not to remember these kinds of events. Michael G. Vann How should Bud Dajo change the way we understand the Philippine-American War and the broader US presence in the Philippines? Should this be taught as foreign policy, military history, colonial history, or American history? Kim Wagner One of my arguments is that there is a direct line from settler violence and westward expansion to Bud Dajo. Some of the senior officers at Bud Dajo were actually veterans of the last stages of the so-called Indian Wars. A couple had been present at Wounded Knee, and it was commonplace to compare to the Moros to the Apache. At the same time, Americans were deliberately studying how European empires administered Muslim populations. Bud Dajo sits at the intersection of an American tradition of settler violence and European imperialism. It is a particularly brutal convergence. So this is US history, imperial history, military history, and colonial history all at once. Interestingly, the Moros did not necessarily see themselves as Filipinos, so Bud Dajo also sits at the margins of the conventional Philippine-American story. It belongs to several intersecting histories that are too often kept separate. Michael G. Vann What role did Islam and anti-Muslim attitudes play in the way American soldiers, politicians, and journalists understood the Moros? Kim Wagner I began this book before the US withdrawal from Afghanistan, so I was very much thinking about the “war on terror.” What struck me were the historical continuities — some headlines about Bud Dajo could have been taken from American newspapers a century later. The anecdote that Donald Trump told about General John J. Pershing and the use of bullets dipped in pig’s blood is actually an oblique reference to the campaigns against the Moros — and American officers did use pig’s blood as a type of spiritual warfare against the Moros. So the discourse about what Trump referred to as “radical Islamic terrorism” is straight out of the colonial playbook. The Americans inherited much of it, not from the Spanish so much as from the British and the Dutch. This playbook held that Muslims constituted a particular type of enemy against whom ordinary weapons were ineffective and normal rules of war did not apply. Leonard Wood, when pressed to explain why US forces had wiped out hundreds of men, women, and children, said they fought as fanatics and did not wish to live. That is almost identical to later narratives about suicide attackers and in the American context, this way of thinking comes from the campaigns against the Moros. The logic is that Muslims are irrational, superstitious, intractable, and implacable; violence is supposedly the only language they understand. That is a self-fulfilling political strategy with an inevitable outcome. Michael G. Vann What do you hope readers take away from Massacre in the Clouds about history and accountability? Kim Wagner There is real value in recovering a forgotten atrocity. I was surprised that no American historian had really done this before. Bud Dajo is probably one of the best visually documented colonial massacres in history, yet it became almost a nonevent in the historical record. So establishing the facts matters in a very basic sense. But I also wrote the book so that it wouldn’t be so easy for Americans to say, “I never knew.” This is, I should add, not about guilt-tripping. I do not think guilt or shame are especially useful ways of engaging with the past. We are not responsible for the past, but we are responsible for what we choose to remember and what we choose to forget. When we choose to forget atrocities like the Bud Dajo Massacre, exceptionalist myths persist — and we can see how that is playing out right now. Michael G. Vann Your previous work has examined British colonial violence in India — the Thuggee campaigns , 1857, Amritsar . Why turn to American colonial violence? Kim Wagner From a historical perspective, the parallels made sense. After working on the British Empire for a long time, I looked at what Americans were doing in the Philippines and saw many similarities. US history needs to be contextualized globally — as a growing number of scholars have shown in recent years. These broader connections and comparisons are crucial if we want to move beyond the conventional national framing of the past. But there is also the issue of American exceptionalism. Americans, and I’m obviously generalizing here, often find it difficult to face violent moments in their past without falling back on justifications: “This is not who we are,” or “I no longer recognize my country.” There is a kind of denial of reality that I thought was important to engage with. Since I am a historian, that is how I do it. History is not just a nerdy hobby. It helps us see the present — however uncomfortable that might be.
