articles.title: For 60 Years, The Battle of Algiers Has Inspired Resistance
articles.author: Luca Peretti
articles.content: Even before Gillo Pontecorvo’s The Battle of Algiers premiered at the Venice Film Festival on August 31, 1966, the film had generated a lot of buzz. The jury presided over by Italian writer Giorgio Bassani gave the film the Golden Lion, the main award of the festival, “for the courage with which it tackled such a difficult and highly controversial historical and political issue, or for the vigor with which it was able to master such a subject.” Beyond the praise, the film was also met with various polemics, which continued well after its release. The French government’s delegation to Venice refused to attend both the screening and the award ceremony at the end of the festival because, in the words of its head representative (civil servant and author Philippe Erlanger), “we interpret the inclusion of the film in the festival as a sign of hostility toward France.” French film critics — who as always flooded the Italian city for the festival, as they represented the largest group of foreign journalists — did see the film but largely did not speak of it favorably: to mention just one, in Le Monde Yvonne Baby wrote how “Gillo Pontecorvo made the mistake of emphasizing — with irritating intensity (to which the music contributes greatly) — the heroism of the Algerian fighters, and of constantly filming, in close-ups and in a tragic twilight, tense, pained faces whose expressions. . . . evoke no emotion whatsoever.” France was not ready to talk about the Algerian war just four years after the humiliating withdrawal from the North African country. But what is Pontecorvo’s film about, and why does it still make sense to talk about it sixty years later? Pioneers The film largely focuses on a long and emblematic episode of the Algerian War (1954–1962), the eponymous battle in the Algerian capital in 1957. Starting with the French paratroopers’ raid on the house of a small group of militants (most notably Ali La Pointe, one of the leaders of the Algerian National Liberation Front [FLN]), with a flashback the film takes the viewers to La Pointe’s political and guerrilla upbringing. It shows the evolving struggle in Algiers, from learning how to control the Casbah to the attempt to bring the fight to the rest of the city. The coda depicts the largely spontaneous December 1960 riots that would eventually lead to independence in 1962. Starring almost exclusively nonprofessional actors and actresses, shot in a realist, quasi-documentary style entirely in Algiers, it was produced after former Algerian guerrilla fighter turned film producer Yacef Saâdi, who wanted to make a film that glorified the independence war, met with Italian director Pontecorvo and screenwriter Franco Solinas, who were interested in making an anti-colonial film focusing on a paradigmatic and symbolic struggle but able to strike universal chords. Both Italians and Algerians were already working on separate projects when they met in 1964 and decided to join forces. As sometimes happens with art, the result far exceeded their hopes, with The Battle of Algiers becoming an almost instant classic, and a film that enjoys “endlessly renewed contemporary resonance,” as film historian Nicholas Harrison noted . It continues, for example, to be screened and discussed vis-à-vis Palestine and as an example of how urban guerrilla tactics can still be applied in contemporary wars. New aspects and new protagonists of the film are also discovered or rediscovered: the cover of Jeremy Harding’s recent book Analogue Africa features a photo of the Algerians and Italians working together on the film (among others, cinematographer Marcello Gatti), and we can also spot a young Sarah Maldoror, only recently recognized as one of the pioneers of anti-colonial and African cinema. The Making of the Film Algiers had just finally become independent when Saâdi created a film production company (Casbah Films) and started planning to make a film on the liberation war. France, which had colonized Algeria in the 1830s and considered it an integral part of its own national territory, did not want to let it go after having lost most of its colonies, including neighboring Morocco and Tunisia and, after a long and bloody war in Indochina. Cinema played its part: filmmakers around the war traveled to Algeria to document the events or made films in solidarity from their countries, and Algerian cinema was born in the flames of the war. Saâdi, backed by the FLN-led government, chose to make a film with Italians precisely because they had been active in solidarity with the Algerians struggling for independence. Pontecorvo wasn’t the first choice, as multiple sources report, but he and Solinas were already working on a project on Algeria, whose working title was Para , which had been in the making since the early 1960s. The two traveled to the country just after independence to look for locations and better understand the Algerian context. After some difficulties finding a producer — Pontecorvo would later tell journalist Irene Bignardi in his interview/memoir that potential producers would tell him “nobody is interested in Arabs or blacks” — the director decided to join forces with Antonio Musu and create their own production company, Igor Film, which joined forces with Casbah Films. Fundraising wasn’t easy: the Italian director and producer risked their own money, while the Algerian government also invested in the film. In June–July 1965, Pontecorvo was already in Algiers, but most likely the actual shooting began in July or August. The dates are important: June 19, 1965, was a landmark day in Algerian history, as with a bloodless coup d’état Houari Boumédiène replaced Ahmed Ben Bella, who had been the first president of independent Algeria. The well-known tale that Algerians saw the tanks in the streets and thought it was the filming of The Battle of Algiers , whereas in fact a putsch was taking place, is probably unrealistic (from the documents we’ve been able to consult so far it seems that the shooting started after that date). Nonetheless, this episode speaks plenty to how important and deeply felt the film was in Algiers during its making. Hundreds of Algerians joined in as extras, the city was used as a location for months (the shooting ended in December), and newspapers enthused about it, “The city was offered to Gillo and his crew as though it were an immense set populated with interesting faces, some of whom came to be selected as extras and for small roles,” wrote Bignardi. The shooting was itself a major event in Algeria in the second half of 1965, at the same time as other Algerian films were being made, and the national cinema was being restructured and reorganized in terms of production but also distribution and the creation of new film institutions. The film was edited and postproduced in the first half of 1966, first by neorealist editor Mario Serandrei and then, after his sudden death, by the young Mario Morra. Unsurprisingly, when in June 1966 the film was screened for the first time in Algiers for its world premiere (ahead of Venice), in the presence of the Algerian authorities but also of those who starred in the movie, it was met with great enthusiasm. Loris Gallico, the Algiers correspondent of the Italian Communist Party daily l’Unità , noted how the film was also “an excellent example of collaboration between Algerians and Italians.” In fact, without overdoing it with an Italian-centered narrative, we can say that Pontecorvo’s film (and others produced by Saâdi’s Casbah Films) was instrumental in forming a group of film people who would then play a major role in shaping Algerian cinema. As Joan Mellen wrote, only a small crew of Italians traveled to Algeria: “The remainder of those who worked on the film were Algerians who, never having worked on a film before, were trained on the spot in various specialties. This, of course, was the intention of the Casbah Film Company, which saw the collaboration with the Italians as a means of training their own film people.” To mention just two beside Saâdi and the uncredited Maldoror, Moussa Haddad worked as assistant director (he would then make several Algerian films) and Ali Maroc, perhaps one of the most important Algerian photographers and directors of photography, was chosen as assistant camera operator. Several nonprofessional actors were chosen for small roles, but also for the role of Ali La Pointe (Brahim Hadjadj); left-wing French theater actor Jean Martin played Colonel Mathieu: he is usually mentioned as the sole professional actor in the film, but small roles were also performed by the great Algerian comedic actor Rouiched and the little-known Italian actor Franco Morici (who was uncredited). A Diplomatic Affair The months prior to the Venice screening saw intense diplomatic maneuvering between France and Italy (and to a lesser extent Algeria), visible in the press and in the archives of their respective foreign ministries. Film festivals were diplomatic events where national cultural authorities submitted the films for consideration, rather than them being picked by a selection committee. In Venice in 1966, however, film director Luigi Chiarini (the founder of the Italian film school during the Fascist period who remained active and powerful in postwar Italy) and his team could issue a small number of direct invitations. This is just what happened to Pontecorvo’s film that year: the official Italian film was Un uomo a metà by Vittorio De Seta (which was “officially nominated for the competition”), while Algeria had no official representation. The political and diplomatic polemics had started much earlier. When the script was submitted to the Italian minister of tourism and entertainment in order to access public funding, the evaluation board noted: “We understand that French circles have reacted to the news of this film. We do not know, however, exactly what kind of reactions these are.” The presence of the film at the Venice film festival was considered by French authorities an “unfriendly act” but no real veto was ever imposed. This was also the long-standing consequence of Italy’s position on the Algerian War: Italian governments and Ente Nazionale Idrocarburi (ENI), the Italian oil and gas public company, expressed direct or indirect support for Algerians while never really breaking with France. French authorities made requests to delete scenes seen as “against” France, like those that depict torture. Ahead of the screening in Venice, Amintore Fanfani, the minister of foreign affairs, wrote to none other than Prime Minister Aldo Moro (later kidnapped and killed by the Red Brigades): “The reactions from Paris, at this moment, are not completely reassuring.. . . . I would be very grateful if you would consider the possibility of personally intervening with my colleague Corona [the minister of culture at the time] and with the Biennale’s Presidency. . . . ”, the Biennale being the institution that organizes the Film Festival and the other major such events (arts, architecture) in Venice. During the festival, when it became a concrete possibility that The Battle of Algiers would win the Golden Lion, Fanfani even sent a message to the prime minister advising against it getting the main award. Finally, during the making of the film and after, Saâdi and Pontecorvo had a complicated relationship with French authorities: in September 1966 the former guerrilla fighter was denied entry to France, while an internal memo of the Cannes Film Festival termed him the “head of the Algerian terrorists.” Pontecorvo, who was Jewish, had fled to France after the Italian Racial Laws were enacted in 1938 and was deeply influenced by French culture: despite this, he was also expelled and readmitted to the country only after an appeal. Pleading his case, he wrote a passionate letter, today preserved among his papers at the Turin Film Museum. A Nomadic Work After receiving the main award in Venice, the film immediately gained cult status. Different factors contributed to this, from the fact that Algiers had become the so-called capital of the Third World (a city where revolutionaries from half of the Global South found a home), to the 1968 protests and movements that embraced the film and widely screened it. This was notably the case of the Black Panthers and other US radical groups: this was, after all, “the film that in the late 1960s was required viewing and something of a teaching tool for radicalized Americans and revolutionary wannabes opposing the Vietnam War.” In a piece from the time, Black organizer and militant Francee Covington wrote that “If [Frantz Fanon’s] The Wretched of the Earth is the ‘handbook for the Black revolution,’ then The Battle of Algiers is its movie counterpart.” The film has often been examined via the ideas and practice of the Algerian-Martinican psychiatric and political leader, Fanon. The Black Panthers showed it hundreds of times: it was even cited as evidence in a trial against the group, because it was contended that it was “used for training purposes by the Black Panthers and required viewing for all members.” As Algiers became the Mecca of Revolution , “the film by Gillo Pontecorvo [did] much to promote the image of Algeria and its liberation war throughout the world,” in the words of Algerian film historian Ahmed Bedjaoui: among others, one could find among Pontecorvo’s personal papers an invitation to screen the film in postrevolutionary Cuba. In Italy, the film was a box office hit despite being hotly challenged by the country’s far right. In one case, upon a rerun of the film in 1972, Rome’s Nuovo Olimpia cinema was assaulted by a group of neofascists, seriously injuring one of the spectators. Predictably, its presence in France was yet more complicated. The film was never formally censored by the French board of film censorship. Rather, as Andrea Brazzoduro reports in his book on French veterans’ memories, it was “a victim of the complex mechanisms of self-censorship and repression that shape the French attitude toward the memory of the war.” Eventually, in 1970–71, the film was screened in theaters in France and seen by thousands, but the cinemas and organizations that screened the film were also attacked both verbally and physically, as Benjamin Stora and Patricia Caill é note. But then the film largely disappeared from both the big and small screen in France, and only at the beginning of the 2000s, when it was shown on TV could most people finally see The Battle of Algiers . Sixty years on, The Battle of Algiers is not only one of the films that best portrayed a historic anti-colonial struggle. More than that, as Andre Nette writes in a new book on political cinema , “one of the most arresting aspects of watching Gillo Pontecorvo’s La battaglia di Algeri over half a century after its release is how contemporary the images of Western soldiers involved in a bloody counterinsurgency campaign in an Arab country feel today.” When the Pentagon screened it in 2003 , during the Iraq War, it was to study guerrilla techniques. And if countless university courses include the film in their programs, it is because it still helps foster discussions on violence and national independence, anti-colonialism and political Islam, and much more. These issues will not be losing their topicality any time soon. We may be talking about this film for many decades more.

articles.title: Statement on the Theft of Our Bus Stop Benches
articles.author: Wilmington DSA
articles.content: We are issuing the following statement regarding the theft and defacement of bus stop benches by a local hate group, as well as the confiscation of benches by the North Carolina Department of Transportation (NCDOT) following Commissioner Dane Scalise’s promise to get in the way of mutual aid efforts to provide a place for all to rest. We will also take the opportunity to further contextualize this situation. A key aspect of Democratic Socialism is the practice of mutual aid, which aims to share resources without seeking profit, build solidarity, and ultimately lead to community self-determination. Repurposing the waste of Capitalism by collecting discarded lumber and paint and inviting neighbors to improve their community is mutual aid. The messages on our benches are an expression of solidarity with the city and people in it. The physical structure is a material good to improve the lives of those living here. Our name is as essential to the benches as anything else. DSA doesn’t dictate the hopeful messages that are painted on our benches as some form of advertising; they come from the hearts of the community members who come to our public bench paints. The benches exist because we believe socialism means working together to give everyone the means to secure their own agency and dignity. This means a right to housing, medical care, education, fast and reliable public transit and yes, the right to a place to sit and rest in public. The benches are not a secret advertisement for Democratic Socialism; the benches themselves are the product of Democratic Socialism. The bench that was stolen, repainted and then posted online had the following messages: “Socialism is Slavery” and “Socialists want to take everything that you have except your job.” Disagreements aside, we appreciate the irony that the vandals could only display their message on a bench built by socialists which they proceeded to “take” instead of building something on their own. We had no plans to pursue a single bench used in an internet stunt, especially since it did not seem as though the bench was actually left for commuters to use. That serves no one, especially the individuals who used that bench to get to and from work, or around the city. If the bench is, indeed, at a new location, we hope it is able to be used by people who need it. Following this theft, Dane Scalise, vice-chair of county commissioners, requested permission from NCDOT for the County to remove all benches to avoid “vigilantism” and “lawlessness.” As of this morning, NCDOT has removed many of the benches on state right-of-way. It is noteworthy that Scalise offered no solutions to the transit issues in our city, just the removal of material goods that had been in place for up to 15 months without issue until now. Barely concealing his political motives, Scalise went so far as to suggest he will do everything in his power to prevent Wave from “partnering” with the DSA. He makes it apparent that he’d prefer transit riders to stand rather than sit on a bench built by socialists. Holding up the actions of a small group of fascists as a justification is only punishing the people of Wilmington for the actions of an isolated minority. We want to be clear: these people are not concerned with public safety; they are concerned with denying a service to the community because they’re scared of the theory it is born out of. They are scared of a world where everyone has their needs met, because that is a world where they have no power. This project is not intended to empower either political party, as we are not affiliated with either. We are first and foremost dedicated to empowering the people of Wilmington. Many of the actors in this situation are claiming to be acting out of genuine concern for community safety. However, any member of the city or county government that lives in Wilmington would have seen these benches. If they had truly been concerned, they could’ve easily learned who made them and reached out. To pretend otherwise is willful ignorance. Our name was on them; we did not hide this program. It was open to the public, advertised heavily, and we wanted the community to participate. Scalise’s actions in particular play directly into the hands of the group that stole the bench. Whether he did this intentionally or through genuine ignorance is irrelevant. He should be voted out as soon as possible, unless he chooses to apologize to transit riders of Wilmington by tendering his resignation immediately so that he can be replaced by someone more willing to serve the people they represent. We acted because we want to highlight the contradiction between what people can do with small resources and what hasn’t been done by those with ample resources. This city and county have the money and resources for improvements. The state of public transit in Wilmington and New Hanover County is not set in stone. It comes from policy decisions, made by our elected leaders, and carried out by staff. That means it can be changed. Anyone who is telling you otherwise, or telling you they are helpless and that you just need to vote more, is lying to you. If you appreciate our work, please come build and paint benches with us, and join our letter campaign demanding that Commissioner Dane Scalise and the rest of the county commissioners call for NCDOT to allow our benches to be returned to the community or otherwise take immediate steps to provide official non-hostile seating for the people of Wilmington.

Following that: the demands in a campaign need to be widely and deeply felt, definable, specific, measurable, and significant enough to actually change peoples’ lives. Also noted was the fact that often the choice of campaign target is as important as the issues chosen for the campaign–campaign targets should be people who are within reach of the workers and who are decision-makers. Finally, the plenary emphasized that escalating the campaign requires buy-in from coworkers at every stage. The campaign should only be escalated when your coworkers are ready for the next step. Discussion touched on stress tests, the mechanics of escalation, and the tact necessary to organize workers who are on visa or are undocumented. articles.title: Jonathan Demme’s Wild, Humanist Cinema Deserves a Reappraisal
articles.author: Eileen Jones
articles.content: There’s a Criterion Channel series paying tribute to director Jonathan Demme that, as short as it is, makes clear that Demme is due for a major reappraisal. It includes only four films — Something Wild (1986), Married to the Mob (1988), The Silence of the Lambs (1991), and Rachel Getting Married (2008) — but each demonstrate both his confidence in mixing genre elements freely as well as his commitment to centering his films on engrossing characters and the actors who play them. This means his early movies especially seem loose and rangy but also kinetic and exciting. Much like his peers Peter Bogdanovich, Francis Ford Coppola, and Martin Scorsese, Demme started his career shooting exploitation movies like Caged Heat (1974) and Crazy Mama (1975) for producer Roger Corman. He found an early champion in critic Pauline Kael, who began the trend of defining Demme as a “humanist” director in the mold of Jean Renoir ( The Rules of the Game ), one who tended to portray a wide range of characters of various classes, races, and backgrounds without condescension, appreciating their struggles and idiosyncrasies. Demme, who died in 2017, soon broke out of the exploitation underground and had a long career with a major influence on contemporary filmmakers. Paul Thomas Anderson was once asked during a Criterion Channel interview what filmmakers had influenced him the most, and he named as his model and hero “Jonathan Demme, Jonathan Demme, and Jonathan Demme.” Even while omitting a few of Demme’s greatest works, such as Melvin and Howard (1980) and the Talking Heads concert film Stop Making Sense (1984), Criterion’s series attests to boldly creative qualities Demme had that seem to be in short supply in recent Hollywood cinema. Demme’s Big Prestige Detour It can be argued that The Silence of the Lambs , Demme’s biggest hit and the film he’s best known for, plus his other Oscar winner Philadelphia (1993), overshadow his livelier, more inventive work. More than one critic has argued that Demme lost his way after this period, with one offering a startling explanation: that Demme the proud progressive was so distressed by LGBTQ-advocacy groups’ protests over Silence of the Lamb ’s cross-dressing serial killer Jame Gumb that he spent years anxiously trying to shore up his progressive bona fides. His attempts to “atone” included Philadelphia , featuring Tom Hanks as an attorney with AIDS. A “passionate liberal Hollywood drama” seemingly designed to win awards, Philadelphia is a well-made film that “never quite transcended the message movie category.” Demme also made a “stilted and overly ‘poetic’” adaptation of Toni Morrison’s Beloved (1998), which bombed even with Oprah Winfrey in the lead. Both films are more “classic” prestige studio projects, reining in Demme’s freewheeling tendencies. Though even when filming in a chillier, more controlled style, Demme and longtime cinematographer Tak Fujimoto created memorable imagery, such as an inventive variation on Demme’s “ signature shot ” in which characters speak directly into the camera: The subjective close-up, where a character addresses the other person in a scene while staring straight into the lens [is] a rarely deployed piece of film grammar, thanks to its disruptive, fourth wall–smashing qualities. But Demme employs the technique to quite the opposite effect: he uses it to create intimacy. This shot was used most powerfully in The Silence of the Lambs , where it transforms the encounters between Jodie Foster’s Clarice Starling and Anthony Hopkins’s Hannibal Lecter: They share barely ten minutes together on screen, but so intense are their conversations, and so close is the camera to the actors’ faces, that it feels half the movie is just them talking. Demme’s Pre- Silence Genius To get a bead on Demme’s more adventurous filmmaking pre– Silence of the Lambs , it helps to go back to one of his earlier breakout films, such as Something Wild . An astutely reconceived screwball comedy with a bopping rhythm keeping time with the infectious and liberatory reggae score, Something Wild is about the transformative impact on a repressed corporate cog named Charlie Driggs (Jeff Daniels) when he meets a free spirit with a dramatic Louise Brooks bob who calls herself Lulu (Melanie Griffith). Almost immediately, he gets pulled along in her sexy, lawless, adventuresome wake. This includes constant shifts in identity and appearance typical of screwball comedy, a genre in which spontaneous role-playing is both a way to revive people who’ve been leading deadened lives and a way to zigzag through the fast-paced, obstacle-filled, deeply insane modern world. Lulu has the endearing zaniness and spontaneity of a “madcap heiress” type such as Carole Lombard in My Man Godfrey or Katharine Hepburn in Bringing Up Baby , but Demme brings her down to earth by giving her working-class roots, a realistically troubled past when she was actually named Audrey, and a dangerous ex-con ex-husband named Ray Sinclair who’s obsessed with her (Ray Liotta). This was Liotta’s first major role and practically steals the film with his electrifying turn as Ray, a menace with a sharklike smile who once shared an edgy outlaw life with then wife Lulu/Audrey. Meeting Ray at Lulu/Audrey’s high school reunion, Charlie picks exactly the wrong time to commit himself to wild Lulu-like ad-libbing, spinning fantastical tales about his new romance that Ray knows are lies. The tension ratchets up to excruciating levels as Ray circles the oblivious, nattering Charlie, radiating lethal vibes, and the screwball-comedy-turned-road-movie shifts into scary thriller terrain. Demme’s political consciousness was reflected in his view of what Something Wild was really about after he read the refreshing E. Max Frye script: It kept surprising you at every twist and turn, and there was this theme of the flipside of putting on your neat suits and committing a certain kind of financial violence as a successful yuppie in a corporation. The dark side of that is a guy like Ray Liotta, who resorts to a more fundamental kind of violence to solve his problems and to get ahead. I liked this collision and I liked what the script said about violence. Something Wild helped to salvage Demme’s career after the disastrous production of Swing Shift (1984) threatened to bring its momentum to a complete halt. With Swing Shift , Demme went up against entrenched star power in the form of Goldie Hawn — still hot off her own daffy hit Private Benjamin (1980) — and lost. According to most accounts, Hawn — who was also producing the film, which costarred her longtime life partner Kurt Russell — watched Demme’s initial cut of the film and hated it. So did the studio executives at Warner Brothers. The film was completely recut and some reshoots were ordered to put the focus more squarely on the narrative arc of Hawn’s character, Kay Walsh. Ironically, this weakened what had been closer to an ensemble film, with several major characters — played by a marvelous cast including Christine Lahti, Holly Hunter, and Fred Ward — caught up in a familiar historical development of World War II: women entering factory jobs to replace the men who had gone off to fight and discovering, through the highest-paying work they had ever done, the joys and challenges of financial and personal independence. When the war ended, those same women were pushed out of their jobs as part of a national campaign insisting that their patriotic duty was to return to the domestic sphere and make way for the returning GIs. The studio cut also sanitized the importance of Kay’s affair with a trumpeter in a local band (Kurt Russell) and its impact on her marriage to a GI (Ed Harris). The new emphasis was on Kay’s remorse and her return to her husband, rather than on how much she has grown as a person — and how that growth suggests she has outgrown him. Hawn insisted that the changes she and the studio wanted were simply meant to clarify the main storyline, but it’s hard not to see a second motive: protecting her star image and her “likability” with audiences who might view Kay’s affair as simply immoral. This drastically reedited version bombed with both critics and the public. Demme’s cut, which is still not available through any official channels, has been declared a masterpiece by the few who’ve seen it. Accounts of its intricately interwoven plot strands, with several characters influencing and shaping one another’s stories, fit with Demme’s broader tendencies as a filmmaker. He had a particular gift for bringing colorful characters to the foreground, whether in small but brilliantly cast pivotal roles or even brief bits, until audiences felt they could follow almost any of them into a completely different but equally engrossing film. Demme’s Improvisational Genius You can see this kind of multicharacter narrative edited in 2008’s Rachel Getting Married , when Demme turbocharged his earlier filmmaking tendencies by borrowing some of the methods and raw aesthetics of the Danish avant-garde movement known as Dogme 95 . Shooting in sequence without a preplanned shot list, Demme filmed a multiday family gathering with such a commitment to realism, Rachel Getting Married was described as a “beautiful home movie” that just so happened to be an actual movie starring Anne Hathaway. Of course, the very first Dogme 95 film, The Celebration (1998), directed by Thomas Vinterberg, felt more like a very unbeautiful home movie. Vinterberg’s film is about a traumatic family gathering to celebrate the sixtieth birthday of the rich patriarch who gets accused by his son of sexually abusing his own children. The plot of Rachel Getting Married also swirls around family trauma, involving the Buchmans, an affluent clan headed by a music industry mogul and devoted family man played by Bill Irwin, the Cyclops from Christopher Nolan’s The Odyssey . The whole clan is triggered by the arrival of one erratic, resentful, guilt-ridden, drug-addicted family member — ex-model Kym (Anne Hathaway). She’s let out of rehab just long enough to attend the wedding of her sister Rachel (Rosemarie DeWitt), who’s the beloved family favorite. Tunde Adebimpe, Anna Hathaway, and Rosemarie DeWitt star in Rachel Getting Married . (Clinica Estetico) After the shoot, the actors all marveled at how much making Rachel Getting Married felt like attending an actual wedding, wearing mics and staying in character throughout, laughing, chatting, drinking, dancing to the live music of various musicians drawn from Demme’s vast music world connections like Robyn Hitchcock from the Soft Boys and TV on the Radio’s Tunde Adebimpe, who plays Sidney Williams, the groom. Meanwhile Demme’s multiple cameras prowled around among them all getting long takes of their often totally unscripted and unrehearsed interactions. This kind of improvisation was definitely central to the project — even the real-life musicians were improvising the score on the spot. They played so incessantly that Anne Hathaway complained about the noise during an intense scene of family confrontation. In the spirit of the project, Demme told her to have her character Kym do something about it. Hathaway then ad-libbed a snappish line to the actor playing her father: “Can you tell them to knock it off?” This kind of risk-taking by a major, established director is a rare thing, especially today, and Demme’s approach generally produced great performances, sometimes career bests. Hathaway, for instance, has never again created so raw, intense, and nerve-wracking a character as Kym. Every one knows how Anthony Hopkins reached a late-career peak of stardom with his indelible Hannibal Lecter, but just look at the work Jason Robards did under Demme’s direction, with his portrayal of a wild-haired and deeply strange but oddly likable Howard Hughes in Melvin and Howard , perhaps his very best performance. And then later, in just a few scenes, as the elderly senior partner in a top law firm in Philadelphia where Robards is terrifically powerful and concentrated, conveying the phony bonhomie and sick-souled malice underneath it all. The Women of Demme’s Cinema Demme had a special talent for working with women, and he repeatedly brought out the best in such actors as Melanie Griffith, Jodie Foster, and Michelle Pfeiffer. He acknowledged that one of his primary drives as a director was an unusual one — making women-centered films: Ever since my days of working with Roger Corman, and perhaps before that, I’ve been a sucker for a woman’s picture. A film with a woman protagonist at the forefront. A woman in jeopardy. A woman on a mission. These are themes that have tremendous appeal to me as a moviegoer and also as a director. I still remember seeing Pfeiffer playing the lead in Demme’s zany gangster comedy Married to the Mob , and — being no fan of Pfeiffer at that point — feeling startled at how charming and funny she was. Playing Angela De Marco, she’s the only big-haired mob wife of the whole Long Island bunch who’s miserable about her seemingly luxurious life because “everything we own fell off the back of a truck” and it’s all, of course, tainted with blood. She’s married to Frankie “the Cucumber” De Marco (Alec Baldwin), the handsomest of the goons working for the local don, Tony “the Tiger” Russo (Dean Stockwell). A perpetual horndog whose only real fear is his jealous wife, Connie (Mercedes Ruehl), Tony murders Frankie when he catches him with one of his girlfriends. Immediately after that, at the funeral, he’s making aggressive passes at newly widowed Angela, who rebuffs him and tries to strike out on her own, free of the mob. At one point, she tells her neighbor Mike Downey (Matthew Modine), who’s actually an undercover FBI agent trying to bring Tony to justice, about her travails, especially being relentlessly pursued by Tony. She says, “I guess he’s been trying to screw me ever since,” and at the word “screw” Pfeiffer crossed her eyes, an endearing way of conveying Angela’s embarrassment, disgust, and incredulity at the madness of her own situation. Michelle Pfeiffer stars in Married to the Mob . (Orion Pictures) “Now I see why she’s a star,” I thought then. And that wasn’t the only time. Melanie Griffith’s star qualities — the matter-of-fact sense of vast sexual experience, the strange, raspy little voice — were perfectly showcased in Something Wild and rarely if ever presented as effectively again. There’s one moment demonstrating Demme’s devotion to actors and performance that sums up all the rest. At the end of Married to the Mob , he includes a series of shots of actors performing in character that, for whatever reason, didn’t make the final cut of the film. But Demme clearly wanted these moments to be seen and appreciated anyway. My favorite one shows Dean Stockwell, as ever-stylish, impeccably dressed, and egocentric mob boss Tony Russo, in the simple act of getting out of a car. Stockwell, always an inspired actor, gets out, pauses, and does a little flourish with his hand, as if Tony is presenting himself to the world with a visual “ta-da!” It encapsulates a quality of Tony’s that’s always been there, except when he’s being terrorized by his formidable wife, Connie: he’s always playacting an exaggerated version of the Mafia don. He’s a little overdressed for the part, forever adding some extra flourish of menace or unctuous elegance to his behavior, the perpetual star of his own private movie playing in his head. Demme’s films are full of these moments that crystallize characters, making them startlingly alive. And because, at his best, he let his characters lead the way through offbeat, unpredictable, adventurous plots, his movies remain fresh and vivid in ways that some of our more ponderous filmmakers could learn a great deal from.

articles.title: After Abdul El-Sayed’s Win in Michigan, Progressives Are Preparing for the Next Round Against AIPAC
articles.content: After setting over $ 30 million on fire in Michigan’s Democratic U.S. Senate primary, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) is reportedly plotting round two against progressive epidemiologist Abdul El-Sayed — this time seeking to boost his Republican general election opponent, Mike Rogers. The New York Times reported Wednesday that the pro-Israel lobbying organization, known as AIPAC , ​ “ has told allies that it is considering a major financial campaign to support the Republican Senate nominee in the Michigan general election this fall.” AIPAC said publicly following El-Sayed’s victory over Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Mich.) in Tuesday’s primary that ​ “ our members remain determined to ensure that voters reject Dr. El-Sayed and his radical anti-Israel agenda in November.” Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.), who endorsed and campaigned for El-Sayed, wrote in response to AIPAC’s post-election statement that she appreciates the group ​ “ proving it doesn’t belong in the Dem Party and especially in our primaries.” “ From endorsing Jan. 6 th members to ensuring Congress remains in the hands of a 34 -count felon, AIPAC is an org committed to undermining democracy at home and abroad,” Ocasio-Cortez wrote on social media . ​ “ See you in November.” Rep. Chris Deluzio (D-Pa.) noted that ​ “ a big majority of Americans want the US government to stop sending American dollars to Israel’s reckless regime and to end the war in Iran.” “ Yet AIPAC is threatening to spend to deliver the Republicans a critical Senate seat in Michigan, helping a Trump stooge like Mike Rogers who will keep funding Netanyahu’s wars and do nothing to stop Trump’s Iran war,” said Deluzio. ​ “ This is exactly why so many Democrats like me have rejected AIPAC.” AIPAC cash accounted for around half of all outside spending in the contest between El-Sayed and Stevens — the most expensive Democratic primary in American history. But the organization and its affiliated groups appear to have plenty more resources to devote to the general election, the results of which could decide control of the U.S. Senate next year. The United Democracy Project (UDP), AIPAC’s super PAC, had over $ 80 million in cash in hand at the end of June, according to federal filings . AIPAC is UDP’s primary funder, but the group has also received cash from right-wing billionaires such as hedge fund manager Paul Singer and businessman Haim Saban. During a virtual town hall days before Tuesday’s election, El-Sayed — a vocal opponent of U.S. support for Israel’s genocidal assault on Gaza — dared AIPAC to keep pouring its financial resources into Michigan’s Senate race. “ AIPAC, if you’re listening, burn your money. Come back and burn it again in the general,” said El-Sayed. ​ “ I’m happy to burn your money for you, and then we can get on to the business of governing and asking whether or not our foreign policy ought to be dictated to us by the interests of a foreign government.” This story first appeared at Common Dreams .

articles.title: Hollywood Is Losing Not Just Jobs but Entire Lineages
articles.author: Clara Aranovich
articles.content: The flight of film and television production out of the United States is usually framed in terms of jobs and dollars. And no wonder: entire careers are evaporating at a nauseating rate, with US film and television production down 40 percent in 2024 from its 2022 peak. What gets less attention is a quieter loss: the erosion of an intergenerational workforce.In 2021, I directed an episode of The CW’s Nancy Drew. Like many productions of its scale, it shot in Vancouver. It was an ambitious show — narratively dense with five lead characters, technically demanding with supernatural elements, all within the constraints of a modest broadcast budget. It was also a blast to make. As with most episodic directing jobs, I parachuted in as a short-term transplant, folding into the well-established ecosystem of a multiseason show.While on Nancy Drew, I met Hannah, a script supervisor who stood all of four feet eleven with a voice to match. We spent long days side by side at the monitors, as directors and script supervisors do. Close in age and aligned on which jokes were absolutely hilarious, we became fast friends.“You’re Jim’s girl, aren’t you?” someone asked her one day, referring to her father, a longtime camera operator and cinematographer. This led to stories of being brought to set as a child and coming of age under the watchful guard of a workforce who “knew her when.”I’ve since learned this kind of intergenerational collaboration is not uncommon in Canada, and working in Toronto and Vancouver, I’ve been repeatedly struck by it — along with a pang of envy and grief for our ailing Hollywood. What emerges is an on-set experience buoyed by a network of shared history and continuity passed from older workers to younger ones, not uncommonly in the same family.Before you write this off as garden-variety nepotism, I’d argue it’s actually trade succession, similar to what you see in the building trades. These are not the film industry’s rarefied or glamorous above-the-line roles. They are the physically demanding, highly specialized trades that form the backbone of film and TV production, and in that context the term “nepotism” loses its stink.The benefits of working with multiple generations of craftspeople are impossible to quantify. The combined knowledge, dedication, and identification with craft and community are greater than the sum of their parts.Trades have long functioned this way, at least since the guild era of the Middle Ages. If you grew up around a craft, you absorbed it by default — awakening in a cloud of sawdust or to the sound of a hammer on an anvil, you were a de facto apprentice. But beyond the nuts and bolts of the trade, the younger generation gets to observe the ineffable soft skills of the work and the countenance required for it.It’s for precisely this reason that the Writers Guild of America fought in 2023 to get writers back on set as producers of their own episodes. The new contract restored a version of that expectation — central to how the next generation of writers learns to be showrunners — but only for some shows, after it had fallen away almost entirely during COVID-19.When Nancy Drew wrapped, Hannah and I stayed loosely in touch. Over the next few years, I worked on a handful of shows in different cities — Santa Fe, Atlanta, even Los Angeles — most of which didn’t make it past their first season as the industry contracted. But when I returned to Vancouver for work, I ran into something I hadn’t experienced in a long time: a lot of the same crew members.Among them was Hannah, now with her married name, directing her own shorts between script supervising gigs. I was reunited with an A-camera dolly grip who’d had a baby, and a producer whose son had started in the locations department. It was frankly utopian. “Now this is an industry town,” I thought.But if Vancouver is a true industry town, what does that make Los Angeles? Increasingly, film is becoming an industry in which the decision-makers are headquartered at a distance from production itself — and in that gap, to paraphrase Antonio Gramsci, morbid symptoms appear.When I recently wrote Hannah to get her blessing to tell her story, she replied, “Literally standing next to another second-gen camera op right now. Didn’t know that wasn’t a thing in LA.” Indeed, it is increasingly uncommon in this age of footloose capital, which uproots industries from the communities that built them and sets them down wherever labor comes cheapest, often thanks to tax breaks and government subsidies.A stable industry that treats its workers well does more than reliably turn out art the public loves. It can be a scaffold on which entire generations grow and flourish. It allows workers not merely to make a living but to actually live — to hit life’s milestones with the work as a steady backdrop, marrying and buying homes and raising the next generation with the confidence that the work will still be there for them. It allows older workers to stick around and pass knowledge down as an uncle might on a Saturday afternoon in his garage wood shop.This is the future I dream of for our industry.

articles.title: Unions Can Save Tech Workers and Tech Work
articles.author: Dan Russell
articles.content: A dramatic shift has taken place in the tech industry over the last several years. Industry leaders who once had a reputation as innovative forward thinkers are more familiar as misanthropic paranoiacs. The playful atmosphere of tech offices flush with investment, enjoying luxe catered lunches to attract programming talent, has been replaced by a looming fear that layoffs are just around the corner as artificial intelligence (AI) company executives make repeated public statements that any day now, everyone will be replaced by superintelligent chatbots. The once-sage advice to “learn to code” isn’t heard much these days. One could hardly be blamed for feeling pessimistic about the tech industry. But last May, 2,100 information technology employees at the University of California (UC) voted to join the union of University Professional and Technical Employees (UPTE-CWA Local 9119). Among the reasons for joining, members have pointed to the layoff protections the union won in its last contract, as well as the positive social vision of technology for which organized workers can fight. This was the largest effort to organize technology workers in the history of the US labor movement. While the tech industry might still be new ground for unions, the methods it took to win were familiar as ever. Jacobin contributor and tech worker Aaron Petcoff spoke with Local 9119 President Dan Russell and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) Unit Cochair Max Belasco about the campaign, what it took to win, and how workers can organize to build technology that serves people rather than the bosses. Aaron Petcoff To begin, could you each tell me about what you do for work and your role relative to the union? Dan Russell I’m in IT, so I do desktop support and server administration. I got hired at UC in 2012. I wasn’t represented at the time, and I’d been hoping there would be a union for IT workers at UC; it was one of the reasons I was excited about the job. Then I saw a flyer for UPTE, which was trying to organize IT workers into a new bargaining unit. I came to find out that was not going very well. So I got involved. My role was added to the unit around 2016, and at that point I got on the executive board and on the bargaining team for the contract fight that started in 2016. I was part of the officer team of a reform slate that got elected in 2018. We ran another leadership slate in 2022. Max Belasco I’ve been working at UCLA for fourteen years, since right after I graduated from UCLA. I’m a tech worker too. My title is business systems analyst, but my working title is manager of BruinLearn and clinical IT. I’m in charge of instructional technology and IT infrastructure at the UCLA School of Law, for our instructional technology and our clinical programs. The School of Law runs several clinics that interface with clients and the public — housing justice, support for veterans navigating social services, and an immigrant family legal clinic that provides wraparound immigration services for families at LAUSD’s Robert F. Kennedy schools. My job is to support these clinics — make sure they have computers, printers, wireless, and access to the databases and tools they need to provide quality legal representation. It’s an important feature of how UCLA engages with the public in LA County. When the pandemic hit, I pivoted toward developing workshops and helping faculty with varying levels of digital literacy use remote instructional technology. I got credentialed in a lot of that technology through EDUCAUSE, and the work became specialized — instructional design, helping law faculty keep their classes Americans with Disabilities Act–compliant, things like that. Eventually UCLA wanted to spin that work off into a nonunion title. I was in a union position, and it wanted to roll up what I was doing into a new title and asked me to apply for it, calling it a promotion — but it would take me out of the bargaining unit. So it was a decision: keep progressing in my career, or go back to square one at the help desk. I chose my career, and I’ve been telling people I’ve regretted it ever since — I lost a lot of the contract protections, I lost out on raises that colleagues who stayed union caught up to within a year, and I pay more in health care premiums. I found that frustration in a lot of other folks too — this two-tier system where some unionized tech workers like Dan benefit from the collective bargaining agreement, but others like us, who have similar specialties and work side-by-side with them, have a much worse tier of benefits and more precarity. That’s not how you build long-term longevity or institutional memory. The stellar contract UPTE won really motivated us to think about what it would mean for all of us if we didn’t have to worry about the layoffs we keep reading about in the private sector — if we could get raises that keep up with inflation, pay less on health care, and actually have a voice in our workplace. That was a big galvanizing moment: we should come together and join a union that’s shown it’s out there fighting for tech workers. Aaron Petcoff I’m curious to learn more about the contract. Max, you’ve already hinted at the layoff protections it secured. What else did the contract win, when was it won, and what’d it take? Dan Russell The raises were pretty huge. A lot of folks were left behind by inflation during the pandemic. I think it was 22 percent over three years. Members save up to $300 a month on health insurance premiums. On layoffs: we got a commitment that before someone is laid off, if there’s a vacant position they’re qualified for, they’d be offered it. And we expanded the existing preferential rehire rights from your own campus to any UC campus. That’s especially appealing for people who can work remotely. It doesn’t matter if you’re at UC San Diego or UC Sacramento. That’s a big thing for tech workers. Aaron Petcoff Max, can you talk about how the contract and those protections played into some of your organizing conversations? Max Belasco Practically speaking, unionized and nonunion tech workers were treated very differently at UCLA, and I saw it when I was in the bargaining unit. UCLA restructured the main IT unit into what was supposed to be a more dynamic model it called Reimagine IT. Functionally, it recreated the entire org chart and forced everyone to reapply for their jobs. If you weren’t hired, you would essentially be laid off. That was terrifying for a lot of my colleagues. UPTE won a big victory there. It organized and got the concession that any represented IT worker in UPTE didn’t have to reapply. They got to keep their jobs and placed into the new org chart. But a large number of people still had to reapply. One person I spoke to during this campaign had to interview four times for the job they already had. When I left the bargaining unit last year, UCLA announced it was going to do another reorganization to bring all the IT units — the law school, central campus, everything — into one thing called One IT. That’s when I started talking with colleagues, and our thought was: When does this stop? Executives, CEOs, and management consultants are making these unilateral decisions about how services should be performed without any input from the people who actually provide them day to day and know how staff, students, and faculty use the technology. Unionization gave us a way to say: this is a widely unpopular way of dealing with our livelihoods. Many of us came from the private sector and committed to the UC because we believe in its mission. We should be able to have job security and feel secure in our work. That hadn’t been the case at UCLA for a while. The conversations with colleagues were about what it would mean if, instead of worrying every two or three years about a reorganization and reapplying for our jobs, we had a contract that said, before you could even be considered for a layoff, you’d get a shot at a vacant position anywhere in the UC system. What would it mean to have actual career-progression guidelines, where you could seek promotion in your department instead of hopping around? What would it mean to get steady raises you could plan a life around — to buy a car, move, or start a family? It was a major shift. It made people think about what an alternative could look like where we’re not just producing more code because we’re scared of losing our jobs but because we feel secure enough to experiment and ask how this actually benefits the end user. The contract is really powerful, but what it led to was even bigger conversations about what our work could be: worker-driven, rather than unilateral control from administration. Aaron Petcoff It seems almost inevitable that winning layoff protections expands the unit. It’s such a strong argument for everyone who’s not union to join. Can we go back to what it actually took to win that contract? Dan Russell We used a lot of the same models to win the contract fight and this new organizing drive. It’s nothing revolutionary. It’s organizing-committee models. At each campus, we have a team of respected workers we recruit, figuring out who the organic leaders are. It’s not the Jane McAlevey model exactly, but the model popularized by McAlevey. We bring them together monthly to talk about where we’re at. We started with a survey asking people what they were dealing with and what they wanted, and through our representatives, we had thousands of conversations across the state. A lot of workers told us the union had never actually asked them what they wanted before. It would just email out a bargaining survey the union came up with. So we used our leaders to ask workers directly, built a bargaining survey from that, took it back out through our leadership structure, put together a contract platform, and asked members to ratify it. We took that to the table, and after UC didn’t budge, we came back and asked: Is it time to strike? And ultimately, we had to strike five times to get the contract — five shorter strikes over the span of about a year. I think the first strike was December 2024, and we settled in November 2025. Aaron Petcoff So this contract fight set these new standards and drew 2,100 new people in. Max Belasco I come from a union family, so I look at this contract and think, this is a great deal. But a lot of tech workers don’t have that familiarity. They think there must be a catch. That was the question I got constantly during the contract campaign: What’s the catch? There’s got to be a downside to all of this. For people that we could actually have an honest conversation with, really talk about what their concerns were, people would sign up. But finding those people was a challenge. When you have 2,100 people, many of whom are remote and may not even come into the office at all, it’s sometimes difficult to identify who we could have those conversations with. So we took what we’d learned from the contract campaign about meeting people where they are and realized we’d just have to have thousands of one-on-one conversations. We took that up to the extreme of doing home visits. That is, actually going to people’s homes to have a conversation away from management and away from Zoom and any screens. And some of us — even me — were kind of skeptical about whether we’d able to do this. But we hit up every single tech worker’s house in California at least once, and leaders elsewhere visited colleagues nearby. That was a huge driver of participation, because we did the work of literally knocking on doors. On the last day of the vote, I drove from Santa Monica to Orange County to knock on doors, and when people asked how important it was, I’d say: I drove from Santa Monica to your house right now because I think this is really important. That gesture itself helps people feel like they can have an honest dialogue about the problems in their workplace in a way that’s hard to do over Zoom. Aaron Petcoff It’d be easy for someone to kind of focus on the differences between tech workers in the public sector like you all in this unit and tech workers in the private sector across the rest of the industry. But there’s a lot of challenges that are obviously familiar, not just in tech but for anyone organizing a largely remote workplace. There are lots of methods of overcoming those barriers, but I’ve never heard of anyone doing home visits for tech workers. Dan Russell The home visits were the last phase. We started by building committees, testing our leaders, and seeing who was willing and able to have the hard conversations (over Zoom, at the worksite, on Slack or Teams). We built campus-based committees and a statewide committee. Before the home visits, we brought people together for a kickoff convention in the Bay Area to build camaraderie and bring into the strategy. Then we said: We’ve tried everything else — what do people think about home visits? Nobody was dying to knock on doors, because not everyone is happy to see you. But like Max said, once you got in front of people, a lot of them said, “This sounds great; it’s too good to be true. What’s the catch?” Some took a couple of conversations; you’d get four or five nos before a yes. So a lot of it was building the skills and commitment of the organizing committee. And every time we had a good conversation, we’d ask “Who’s your most respected colleague? Can you set up a meeting?” Everything you can do to use the networks and relationships that already exist is gold. The last thing you want is to drop in on somebody cold. If someone can talk to a person they already trust, you’re half the way there. Max Belasco And in California, there’s card check . Under California state law, for a group our size, two things have to happen. You don’t just need a majority saying yes — you need a majority of everyone in the bargaining unit to vote. So with 2,100 people, if only 500 vote and 251 vote yes, it doesn’t matter; you have to win more than 50-percent-plus-one of everyone in the relevant job titles. That’s a higher standard. You can’t win with 30 percent participation. You could collect cards or survey support, but a controlled vote let us pose it as a clear choice: Do you want these benefits, which you can actually get right now if you vote yes? That made it much easier to talk with colleagues: this isn’t theoretical, this is what we stand to gain by coming together. Aaron Petcoff What were the concerns of people you all spoke with who were still hesitant about voting to join the unit? Max Belasco A few things came up. The biggest barrier was just convincing people that this could actually be done. I think for a lot of people, there was still the hang-up on the idea that tech workers are not union-friendly. I also think that while we didn’t see any formal kind of retaliation, there were some people who wondered how the union could affect their relationship with their manager. But often your direct manager isn’t even the source of your pain. They’re dealing with limited resources, structural problems, and decisions that are made higher up. Another concern was about federal cuts to funding and UC’s budget. If the system is already cash-strapped because of attacks from the federal level, could people get laid off if the union bargained for too much? For me, there’s something touching there, but it also means that UC has created this dynamic where you have people who feel that if they ask for something that they deserve, they’re worried they’re taking it from somebody else. It’s pitting people against each other. It took deliberate work to talk about the resources UC actually has. The system has $26 billion in emergency funds it can pull at any moment. It’s purchased ten hospitals in the past ten years. The money is available. It’s a question of distribution. I think that it was important for the union to talk about how we make sure that the UC prioritizes funding the services and obligations it has to the public, including making sure that frontline workers and professionals are given the proper money and funding that they need. Aaron Petcoff It’s striking how much there is in common between private sector organizing and the experience you all are describing. It’s not uncommon that workers are scared into believing they have to take what they’re offered because a union would force their employer to close down. Max Belasco There are real similarities. And this is something that we see as a result of the siege that the public sector has been under now for decades, in which services are either fully privatized or practices are imported from the private sector. But speaking for myself, I’d like us to be an alternative to what exists in Silicon Valley right now. There’s this myth that the founder is the source of innovation and the rest of us are just here to usher in their product. That’s not why I became a technologist. I believed the story of building something new in a garage that makes people’s lives better. I really think the public sector gives us an opening to build an alternative model. A lot of us put a lot of our time into developing this technical expertise. We want to have some decision-making power over our jobs. I think through that, we can create a more innovative space where people on the front line have a sense of investment. Aaron Petcoff Speaking of Silicon Valley’s vision of the workplace, we should talk about AI. That’s obviously a huge source of anxiety for a lot of workers. Did that come up at all in organizing? Dan Russell What I heard was mostly people worried about layoffs in general. IT workers live in constant fear of being laid off, because it feels easy to get rid of an IT worker. When there are no rules about who you can lay off, the fear of AI becomes, “They’re going to lay me off.” We heard a rumor at Santa Cruz that they’d lay off half the IT department. That didn’t actually happen. But it’s a place that’s seen constant layoffs and reorgs, and people live in that constant fear of being next. AI has just amplified those fears. Max Belasco When I got into IT, the idea was that you were learning technical skills that gave you job security. That’s just not the environment anyone’s working in anymore. The venture capital money has dried up, and people see these mass layoffs at Meta and Oracle and think: What’s going to happen at the UC, this public institution? Because what happens in the private sector often informs the public sector, which is always subject to people wanting to cut costs. So people are concerned about layoffs. It comes down to control. They don’t feel in control of their careers. A lot of people invested time learning these skills and came to UC to use them to help people with a promise of long-term job security, and people are worried that’s going to be betrayed. Aaron Petcoff This sense of insecurity isn’t particular to the UC system, of course. We’ve seen in recent primary elections: voters are very favorable to candidates who speak directly to this general feeling of economic insecurity, frustrations over affordability, and the like. AI adds fuel to those fears. Dan Russell How do you expect people to react when all these tech bros and boosters are saying this will result in 90 percent of workers losing their jobs? If that’s in the New York Times , people take it seriously, even if it’s total bulls — . Aaron Petcoff Did the union put any particular emphasis on AI when reaching out to workers? Did it come up at all as a motivation for joining? Dan Russell I don’t know that we put any focus on AI as much as on the need for job security. Looking back, the thing that drove the urgency around job security in our big contract fight was the Big Beautiful Bill: the threat of cuts to public research and public healthcare funding. AI was more of a threat for the IT campaign specifically, but the bigger-picture threat was cuts to public services, research, health care, and education. That made job security one of the big issues, and it grew when Donald Trump’s cuts came into focus while we were already partway through the contract fight. Fortunately, we already had those things on the table. Our folks on the research and health care sides were asking, are we going to see a 50 percent reduction in UC’s income? UC gets much more of its funding from the federal government than from the state. I believe it’s the biggest or second-biggest recipient of the National Institutes of Health and National Science Foundation grants. If not the majority, it’s the plurality of UC’s funding. So that was honestly a bigger threat to job security than AI. Max Belasco One of the most motivating things at UCLA was the second reorganization, which was billed as a way to save money and was announced right when UCLA was in the federal government’s crosshairs. With AI, it’s come up and been a concern, but most of my colleagues feel that if AI weren’t there, it would be something else. The real concern, as Dan said, is that our careers and livelihoods are caught in this political jousting between the federal government and the universities. It’s become more incumbent on us to have an organization where we can assert our own concerns, whether about our work or the services we support. Aaron Petcoff How do you feel about the general idea of unions in the tech industry at this moment? Max Belasco There’s this popular notion that unions haven’t caught on in tech because they stymie innovation or stop us from being creative. But where we are right now, I don’t think anyone would say that new technology is being developed for the betterment of humanity. In the UC, we have an opportunity to demonstrate an alternative: if you give frontline workers actual say over what they’re doing and let us unlock our creativity by collaborating instead of competing and fearing layoffs, that shows a new dynamic. We can recapture that original vision of innovation: working in a garage with your buds to make something cool that benefits people’s lives. That’s the reason I wanted to become a tech person. Being in the union is actually the best avenue we have to get back to that, and it’s much more real than what we have right now. Dan Russell More than that, technology has made us a lot more productive, and we just haven’t seen enough of the benefits from that. Imagine if we could harness those productivity increases to actually give people the health care they deserve for free, fund research that serves the public interest instead of corporate profits, and provide the education people want. That’s what we should be using technology for: making sure people have what they need. Once they do, we should be able to work less. That’s what technology should be about, whether you create it or you rely on it for patient care, education, or research. Fundamentally, this is about making sure we control the technology so it serves working people instead of being used just to make the worst people in the world even richer. Aaron Petcoff It seems to me that you all are on the front lines in a war against “ enshittification .” You’re showing a way out of this world where everything seems to be lazily getting worse and worse. Dan Russell Public health care, education, and research will keep getting more expensive and worse at the same time. That’s the trajectory we’re on, and we’ve got to reverse it.
